An original-district coefficient is a predicted minute difference from the omitted reference district, adjusted for the baseline predictors. For CV, the small-group merging is geographic and does not use commute time. The merged groups are a practical classroom solution and may combine places with different histories.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?
url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=csv&q=",
              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n
                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))
read_csv(url)


# A tibble: 32 × 2
   text_general_code                 n
   <chr>                         <dbl>
 1 Thefts                        37054
 2 Other Assaults                25986
 3 Motor Vehicle Theft           22478
 4 Vandalism/Criminal Mischief   17346
 5 All Other Offenses            13334
 6 Theft from Vehicle            13002
 7 Fraud                          7661
 8 Aggravated Assault No Firearm  5134
 9 Burglary Residential           3800
10 Aggravated Assault Firearm     3320
# ℹ 22 more rows




Worked example: residential burglaries in 2023


Code
burglary <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))    # Carto returns EPSG 4326; translate immediately

nrow(burglary)


[1] 3800








WarningCheck for missing geometry



Some records have no location. Drop them with filter(!st_is_empty(burglary)), and count how many you lost. Every point you drop is a point that won’t be counted.




Other layers to try
These tables were available on Carto as of this fall. If a query fails, check the dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page for the current table name.

The Week 4 feed



Datasets not on Carto often have a GeoJSON download link on their OpenDataPhilly page. st_read() reads those URLs too. For example, navigage to https://opendataphilly.org/, find a dataset that you’d like to import. I found city landmarks. On the page there is a link to a GeoJSON file. I simply right-clicked on that hyperlink and copied it and then used st_read() and pasted the link:
landmarks <- st_read(“https://hub.arcgis.com/api/v3/datasets/6b2fe4a0fbe14e0a8e6afceaea230b8e_0/downloads/data?format=geojson&spatialRefId=4326&where=1%3D1”)


Your turn
Pull at least two layers that you think relate to your outcome. Base your choice on your Part 2C answer.


Code
layer1 <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"
) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

# Keep only records with geometry and report the number removed
n_burglary_before_geometry_check <- nrow(layer1)
layer1 <- layer1 %>% filter(!st_is_empty(.))
n_burglary_without_geometry <- n_burglary_before_geometry_check - nrow(layer1)

layer2 <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))


Answer: Why these layers? What do you expect them to capture that the ACS variables don’t?
Your answer:
Residential burglary points capture a neighborhood-safety condition, and Indego stations capture proximity to bike-share access. Neither is measured by the ACS predictors, which describe household and population characteristics. I expect these layers to add local context that could help explain commute times, although station distance is only a proxy for the transit options residents can actually use.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.458  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
# Feature 1: count burglaries in each tract
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1)))
f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + n_burglary)
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "burglary count", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Adds 2023 residential burglary count")

# Feature 2: normalize count by tract area
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
                            burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi)
f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + burglary_per_sqmi)
m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "burglaries per square mile", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "Adds area-normalized 2023 burglary count")

# Feature 3: distance to nearest Indego station
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)
nearest_station_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
  st_distance(tract_pts, layer2[nearest_station_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)
f4 <- update(f3, . ~ . + dist_station_mi)
m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "distance to nearest Indego station", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "Adds nearest-station distance in miles")
model_log


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model added                              cv_rmse notes                        
  <chr> <chr>                                <dbl> <chr>                        
1 m1    ACS baseline                          5.13 Mean commute minutes from AC…
2 m2    burglary count                        5.14 Adds 2023 residential burgla…
3 m3    burglaries per square mile            5.16 Adds area-normalized 2023 bu…
4 m4    distance to nearest Indego station    5.17 Adds nearest-station distanc…


Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Your answer:
Among the spatial additions, burglary count has the lowest CV RMSE (5.14 minutes). Compared with the baseline, the spatial model(s) that made CV RMSE worse are m2, m3, m4. Burglary may add only an indirect signal about commuting, and Indego distance does not measure SEPTA service or job destinations, so either could add little or even increase CV error.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-18.5194  -3.0884  -0.0491   2.9256  16.3693 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     25.87577    0.69995  36.968  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi       2.10433    0.25419   8.279 2.19e-15 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2) -0.12422    0.01908  -6.511 2.39e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.054 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1911,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1868 
F-statistic: 44.54 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  79
2 Inner 134
3 Outer 167


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5146  -3.2886  -0.1537   3.1284  17.1430 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  27.5537     0.5699  48.349  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner     4.3575     0.7185   6.065 3.21e-09 ***
ringOuter     6.4529     0.6917   9.329  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.065 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1833 
F-statistic: 43.52 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.




5D: Your turn
Try at least one of each: a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Choose which variables to transform based on your plots, not at random. Log each model.


Code
# Log transform skewed median household income
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(log_income = log1p(median_incomeE))
f_log <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + log_income)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m5", added = "log of median household income",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts), notes = "Replaces raw income with log1p(income)")

# Allow the station-distance relationship to curve
f_sq <- update(f4, . ~ . + I(dist_station_mi^2))
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m6", added = "squared distance to Indego station",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts), notes = "Tests a curved station-distance relationship")

# Compare income quartiles as categories
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(income_group = factor(dplyr::ntile(median_incomeE, 4),
  levels = 1:4, labels = c("Q1_lowest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4_highest")))
f_cat <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + income_group)
m_cat <- lm(f_cat, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "income quartile factor",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_cat, tracts), notes = "Replaces linear income with four income groups")
model_log


# A tibble: 7 × 4
  model added                              cv_rmse notes                        
  <chr> <chr>                                <dbl> <chr>                        
1 m1    ACS baseline                          5.13 Mean commute minutes from AC…
2 m2    burglary count                        5.14 Adds 2023 residential burgla…
3 m3    burglaries per square mile            5.16 Adds area-normalized 2023 bu…
4 m4    distance to nearest Indego station    5.17 Adds nearest-station distanc…
5 m5    log of median household income        5.18 Replaces raw income with log…
6 m6    squared distance to Indego station    5.12 Tests a curved station-dista…
7 m7    income quartile factor                5.16 Replaces linear income with …


Answer: Which transformation helped most? For your categorical variable, write one sentence reading one of its coefficients correctly, naming the reference level.
Your answer:
The transformation with the lowest CV RMSE is squared distance to Indego station (5.12 minutes). In the categorical model, Q1_lowest is the reference group: holding the other predictors in that model constant, Q4_highest tracts are predicted to have 1.5 minutes shorter mean commutes than Q1_lowest tracts.

Part 6: Your final model
Combine the features and transformations that earned their place, judged by CV RMSE, not p-values.

Put your two residual maps side by side, or put them next to each other in the rendered document. Did the clusters from Part 2C shrink? Where did they stay?
The comparison figure places the Part 6 final-model map first and the Part 2C baseline map second. Mean absolute residual changes from 3.95 minutes in the baseline to 3.91 minutes in the final model. title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer:
The best tested addition is squared distance to Indego station; the weakest is log of median household income. Their CV RMSEs are 5.12 and 5.18 minutes; CV error on unseen tracts is the basis for choosing features. In the final model, a one-percentage-point increase in bachelor’s-or-higher share changes predicted commute time by -0.07 minutes, holding other predictors constant. For tract GEOID 42101034701, with bachelor’s share closest to the sample median, the final model predicts 34.51 minutes.
The residual map and the feature comparisons suggest where the model needs more information. A useful next measure would be transit travel time and service frequency to job centers, using SEPTA schedules and Census LEHD/LODES job locations. Burglary is only an indirect measure of neighborhood context, and station distance does not capture routes, transfers, or frequency, so those spatial features can help little even when the underlying idea matters. The correlation between ACS outcome CV and absolute final residual is 0.28. A positive association means larger misses tend to occur where the ACS outcome is less reliable; it would suggest uncertainty contributes to the error, but it would not establish that uncertainty explains all of it. I would also compare the residual map with the reliability plot, since places with reliable ACS estimates can still have large prediction errors when the model omits important local conditions. The log-income model tests whether income has diminishing returns, the squared-distance model allows the station relationship to bend, and the income-group model allows step changes between quartiles. Whichever gives the smallest held-out error earns its place as a predictive feature, even if its coefficient is not statistically significant. These comparisons describe predictive association across tracts, not the causal effect of changing income, education, or infrastructure.

Submitting

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 1: Outcome and reliability

1A: Pull the outcome and baseline predictors
The outcome is B08013_001, aggregate travel time, divided by B08303_001, workers who did not work at home. It describes commuters aged 16 and over; people working at home are outside this denominator. A transportation agency could identify areas where commutes are longer than tract characteristics suggest. Duration is a partial indicator of access: it does not count reachable jobs or capture people who cannot find work.

None is calculated from commute time or its time categories. All enter the baseline without transformations, allowing later changes to be evaluated explicitly.


Show code
philly_tracts <- cached_data("acs_2023", function() {
  get_acs(geography = "tract", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(total_pop = "B01003_001", travel_minutes = "B08013_001",
      commuters = "B08303_001", median_income = "B19013_001",
      pop_25_plus = "B15003_001", bachelors = "B15003_022",
      masters = "B15003_023", professional = "B15003_024",
      doctorate = "B15003_025", occupied_units = "B25003_001",
      renter_occupied = "B25003_003"),
    year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE)
}) %>% st_transform(2272) %>% st_make_valid() %>% arrange(GEOID)




Show code
# Convert negative ACS sentinel values to NA before division.
philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & matches("[EM]$"), ~ if_else(.x < 0, NA_real_, .x)),
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(.), "mi^2")),
    commute_denom = if_else(commutersE > 0, commutersE, NA_real_),
    y = travel_minutesE / commute_denom,
    y_moe = moe_ratio(num = travel_minutesE, denom = commute_denom,
                     moe_num = travel_minutesM, moe_denom = commutersM),
    y_cv = if_else(y > 0, (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100, NA_real_),
    income_k = median_incomeE / 1000,
    ba_share = 100 * (bachelorsE + mastersE + professionalE + doctorateE) /
      if_else(pop_25_plusE > 0, pop_25_plusE, NA_real_),
    renter_share = 100 * renter_occupiedE /
      if_else(occupied_unitsE > 0, occupied_unitsE, NA_real_),
    pop_density_k = total_popE / area_sqmi / 1000,
    reliability = case_when(!is.finite(y_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
      y_cv < 12 ~ "High", y_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate", TRUE ~ "Low"))


The ratio MOE uses named arguments: numerator, denominator, numerator MOE, denominator MOE, following the tidycensus reference. Dividing the 90% MOE by 1.645 approximates a standard error. This derived ratio MOE does not incorporate the full covariance between the two ACS estimates.

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 3: Philadelphia open data
I use 2023 residential burglaries and shooting-victim records. Burglary measures reported property crime near residences; victim locations describe exposure to serious violence. Safety conditions might correlate with travel choices and neighborhood disinvestment after the ACS controls, but this is a hypothesis to test. Neither layer directly measures transit access, and reporting/geocoding differences limit interpretation. A shooting-victim record is a victim, not necessarily a unique shooting incident.


Show code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=",
                 URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}
burglary_raw <- cached_data("burglary_2023", function() carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"))
victims_raw <- cached_data("shooting_victims_2023", function() carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, date_ FROM shootings
   WHERE date_ >= '2023-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"))
city_boundary <- st_union(philly_tracts)
clean_points <- function(x, label) {
  usable <- !st_is_empty(x) & (st_is_valid(x) %in% TRUE)
  located <- st_transform(x[usable, ], st_crs(tracts))
  inside <- lengths(st_intersects(located, city_boundary)) > 0
  list(data = located[inside, ], audit = tibble(layer = label,
    downloaded = nrow(x), missing_or_invalid = sum(!usable),
    outside_city = sum(!inside), retained = sum(inside)))
}
b <- clean_points(burglary_raw, "Residential burglary records")
s <- clean_points(victims_raw, "Shooting-victim records")
burglary <- b$data
victims <- s$data
stopifnot(nrow(burglary) > 0, nrow(victims) > 0)

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 4: Spatial features

4A–4B: Counts and densities
I compare each feature against the same ACS baseline first, isolating its predictive contribution before combinations. Counts retain zeros. Density uses tract polygon area, including any water; large waterfront tracts may have lower density than a land-only measure would imply.


Show code
# Assign boundary points once. Tracts are sorted by GEOID, making ties reproducible.
point_counts <- function(points) {
  hits <- st_intersects(points, philly_tracts)
  idx <- vapply(hits, function(z) if (length(z)) z[1] else NA_integer_, integer(1))
  all_counts <- tabulate(idx, nbins = nrow(philly_tracts))
  all_counts[match(tracts$GEOID, philly_tracts$GEOID)]
}
tracts$n_burglary <- point_counts(burglary)
log_model("m2", update(f1, . ~ . + n_burglary), "Burglary count", "m1")
tracts$burglary_per_sqmi <- tracts$n_burglary / tracts$area_sqmi
log_model("m3", update(f1, . ~ . + burglary_per_sqmi),
          "Burglary density", "m1", "Alternative to raw count")
tracts$n_victims <- point_counts(victims)
tracts$victims_per_sqmi <- tracts$n_victims / tracts$area_sqmi
log_model("m4", update(f1, . ~ . + victims_per_sqmi), "Shooting-victim density", "m1")
# Inspect small denominators although per-capita rates are not modeled.

Four features come from the two downloaded layers, covering count, density, and nearest distance, plus the City Hall feature. Distances are straight-line measurements from an interior representative point, not travel times or population-weighted access. City Hall is a fixed downtown employment proxy; suburban jobs are not represented.
Distance to City Hall is the strongest individual spatial addition: its RMSE is 5.12 minutes, an improvement of 0.03 minutes from baseline (positive means better). Shooting-victim density is the weakest, with an improvement of -0.01 minutes. Counts can reflect tract size; density and nearest distance describe different aspects of the uneven event distribution. Their information can overlap with income and population density already in the baseline.
All four safety features slightly increase RMSE here. Their differences are small, so I interpret them as a lack of demonstrated improvement on these folds rather than convincing evidence of worse performance. The hypothesized safety mechanism does not earn a place in the final model.

Part 5: Transform features

5A: Inspect skew and curvature


Show code
tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(`Burglary density` = burglary_per_sqmi,
            `Log1p burglary density` = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi)) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "scale", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(value)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#287c8e", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free_x") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Tracts")









Show code
ggplot(tracts, aes(dist_ch_mi, y)) + geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#2166ac") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "#b2182b") +
  labs(x = "Distance to City Hall (miles)", y = "Mean commute (minutes)",
       subtitle = "Blue: straight line; red: quadratic (unadjusted)")









The histograms show how the log compresses the density tail, while log1p() preserves zero-event tracts. The distance plot motivates a curve and distance bands: a one-mile increase need not mean the same commute change near downtown and near the city edge. The plot is unadjusted; model comparisons retain all baseline predictors.


5B–5D: Log, squared term, and categorical models


Show code
tracts$log_burglary <- log1p(tracts$burglary_per_sqmi)
f_log <- update(f1, . ~ . + log_burglary)
log_model("m7", f_log, "Log1p burglary density", "m3", "Replace raw density with log1p")
f_sq <- update(f1, . ~ . + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2))
log_model("m8", f_sq, "Squared City Hall distance", "m6", "Retain linear and squared distance")
tracts$ring <- factor(case_when(tracts$dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
  tracts$dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner", TRUE ~ "Outer"), levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
ring_counts <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)
stopifnot(all(ring_counts$n >= 20))

The biggest improvement over the corresponding untransformed model is Squared City Hall distance, improving mean fold RMSE by 0.12 minutes. The log lists the parents: log versus raw density, and quadratic/categorical versus linear distance. In the categorical model, Outer tracts have predicted commutes 4.23 minutes higher than Core tracts, holding the four ACS predictors fixed. The quadratic’s slope at distance x is β₁ + 2β₂x; neither coefficient alone describes the full relationship. For the log1p density term, a change from density a to b changes the prediction by β[log(1 + b) − log(1 + a)], with other predictors held fixed.

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 6: Final model

Combine useful features, then compare
Starting with the baseline, I consider the better count/raw-density/log-density version of burglary, victim density, nearest-victim distance, and the better linear/quadratic/categorical City Hall measure, in that order. I attempt a feature only when its individual candidate beats baseline and retain it in the combination only if it improves the current score. Every attempted combination is logged. This is a small search, not exhaustive subset selection. I choose the lowest RMSE among all evaluated candidates; ties favor the earlier specification.


Show code
best_id <- function(ids) {
  z <- model_log %>% filter(model %in% ids)
  z$model[which.min(z$cv_rmse)]
}
candidate_groups <- list(c("m2", "m3", "m7"), "m4", "m5", c("m6", "m8", "m9"))
current_id <- "m1"
baseline_terms <- attr(terms(f1), "term.labels")
for (i in seq_along(candidate_groups)) {
  id <- best_id(candidate_groups[[i]])
  if (model_log$cv_rmse[match(id, model_log$model)] >= model_log$cv_rmse[1]) next
  extra_terms <- setdiff(attr(terms(formulas[[id]]), "term.labels"), baseline_terms)
  combined <- reformulate(unique(c(attr(terms(formulas[[current_id]]), "term.labels"),
                                    extra_terms)), response = "y")
  combined_id <- paste0("combine", i)
  log_model(combined_id, combined, paste("Add", model_log$added[match(id, model_log$model)]),
            current_id, "Retain only if CV RMSE decreases")
  if (tail(model_log$improvement, 1) > 0) current_id <- combined_id
}
selected_id <- model_log$model[which.min(model_log$cv_rmse)]
f_final <- formulas[[selected_id]]
m_final <- lm(f_final, data = tracts)
final_rmse <- model_log$cv_rmse[match(selected_id, model_log$model)]
baseline_rmse <- model_log$cv_rmse[1]
model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "final", added = paste("Selected", selected_id),
  compared_to = "m1", cv_rmse = final_rmse, improvement = baseline_rmse - final_rmse,
  notes = "Reuse selected candidate's score; no independent test set")
summary(m_final)

The selected model is m8: y ~ income_k + ba_share + renter_share + pop_density_k + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2). Its mean fold RMSE is 4.99 minutes, compared with 5.14 for baseline, a 2.9% reduction. Nested or separate spatial validation would support a stronger generalization claim.
Only the City Hall distance family survives the individual screening. Consequently, combine4 repeats m8 against the baseline; it is not an additional independent result. The final specification keeps the four ACS predictors plus linear and squared City Hall distance. The fitted curve rises and then turns down at about 8.28 miles, within the observed distance range. This is compatible with different commuting patterns toward the city edge, but does not establish where residents work.

The rank correlation between ACS CV and absolute held-out error is 0.17, a weak positive association. The upward smooth and the low-reliability group’s larger mean error support some connection to sampling uncertainty, but large misses also occur at moderate CVs. Only one tract is classified High, so that group’s average is not a stable comparison. The median approximate outcome standard error is 7.01 minutes, exceeding final model RMSE of 4.99 minutes. This does not mean sampling noise explains more than 100% of the error: the ratio-MOE approximation omits covariance, and a median estimated SE is not a decomposition of prediction error. Omitted variables, predictor error, and model misspecification also contribute.

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 7: Reflection
The most useful addition is City Hall distance with its squared term, reducing mean fold RMSE by 0.15 minutes from baseline. The curve allows downtown proximity to matter differently near the center and city edge; a single slope misses that variation. Shooting-victim density disappoints most among individual spatial features: I expected neighborhood safety to add context, but its information may overlap with socioeconomic predictors and it measures travel access only indirectly. All safety additions slightly worsen RMSE; these small differences establish no predictive gain here, not a causal absence of safety effects.
For the coefficient reading, β̂ for median household income is 0.009 minutes per $1,000, holding other final-model predictors fixed. For the prediction reading, otherwise identical tracts differing by $10,000 in median income have fitted commute times differing by 0.09 minutes (higher-income minus lower-income). This is an adjusted association between tract averages, not an individual or causal income effect.
Geographic error remains: West (west of 75.19 W) has the largest final mean absolute held-out error among the descriptive sectors. I would next measure jobs reachable within a fixed travel-time budget and historical transit frequency. Census LEHD Origin–Destination Employment Statistics and archived SEPTA GTFS schedules could represent destinations, transfers, and service availability more directly than safety records or straight-line downtown distance. Matching those inputs to 2023 or earlier remains essential.
Finally, the uncertainty plot rises, but the rank correlation of 0.17 is weak and substantial errors remain at moderate CVs. The median approximate outcome standard error is 7.01 minutes; its size emphasizes uncertainty without identifying its share of model error. The ratio approximation omits covariance, and the five-year ACS spans changing commuting conditions. Reusing folds to choose features can make the final improvement optimistic; independent spatial validation is needed before operational use.

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 1: Outcome and reliability

1A: Pull the outcome and baseline predictors
The outcome is B08013_001, aggregate travel time, divided by B08303_001, workers who did not work at home. It describes commuters aged 16 and over; people working at home are outside this denominator. A transportation agency could identify areas where commutes are longer than tract characteristics suggest. Duration is a partial indicator of access: it does not count reachable jobs or capture people who cannot find work.

None is calculated from commute time or its time categories. All enter the baseline without transformations, allowing later changes to be evaluated explicitly.


Show code
philly_tracts <- cached_data("acs_2023", function() {
  get_acs(geography = "tract", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(total_pop = "B01003_001", travel_minutes = "B08013_001",
      commuters = "B08303_001", median_income = "B19013_001",
      pop_25_plus = "B15003_001", bachelors = "B15003_022",
      masters = "B15003_023", professional = "B15003_024",
      doctorate = "B15003_025", occupied_units = "B25003_001",
      renter_occupied = "B25003_003"),
    year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE)
}) %>% st_transform(2272) %>% st_make_valid() %>% arrange(GEOID)




Show code
# Convert negative ACS sentinel values to NA before division.
philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric) & matches("[EM]$"), ~ if_else(.x < 0, NA_real_, .x)),
    area_sqmi = as.numeric(units::set_units(st_area(.), "mi^2")),
    commute_denom = if_else(commutersE > 0, commutersE, NA_real_),
    y = travel_minutesE / commute_denom,
    y_moe = moe_ratio(num = travel_minutesE, denom = commute_denom,
                     moe_num = travel_minutesM, moe_denom = commutersM),
    y_cv = if_else(y > 0, (y_moe / 1.645) / y * 100, NA_real_),
    income_k = median_incomeE / 1000,
    ba_share = 100 * (bachelorsE + mastersE + professionalE + doctorateE) /
      if_else(pop_25_plusE > 0, pop_25_plusE, NA_real_),
    renter_share = 100 * renter_occupiedE /
      if_else(occupied_unitsE > 0, occupied_unitsE, NA_real_),
    pop_density_k = total_popE / area_sqmi / 1000,
    reliability = case_when(!is.finite(y_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
      y_cv < 12 ~ "High", y_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate", TRUE ~ "Low"))


The ratio MOE uses named arguments: numerator, denominator, numerator MOE, denominator MOE, following the tidycensus reference. Dividing the 90% MOE by 1.645 approximates a standard error. This derived ratio MOE does not incorporate the full covariance between the two ACS estimates.

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 3: Philadelphia open data
I use 2023 residential burglaries and shooting-victim records. Burglary measures reported property crime near residences; victim locations describe exposure to serious violence. Safety conditions might correlate with travel choices and neighborhood disinvestment after the ACS controls, but this is a hypothesis to test. Neither layer directly measures transit access, and reporting/geocoding differences limit interpretation. A shooting-victim record is a victim, not necessarily a unique shooting incident.


Show code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=",
                 URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}
burglary_raw <- cached_data("burglary_2023", function() carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, text_general_code, dispatch_date
   FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
     AND text_general_code = 'Burglary Residential'"))
victims_raw <- cached_data("shooting_victims_2023", function() carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, date_ FROM shootings
   WHERE date_ >= '2023-01-01' AND date_ < '2024-01-01'"))
city_boundary <- st_union(philly_tracts)
clean_points <- function(x, label) {
  usable <- !st_is_empty(x) & (st_is_valid(x) %in% TRUE)
  located <- st_transform(x[usable, ], st_crs(tracts))
  inside <- lengths(st_intersects(located, city_boundary)) > 0
  list(data = located[inside, ], audit = tibble(layer = label,
    downloaded = nrow(x), missing_or_invalid = sum(!usable),
    outside_city = sum(!inside), retained = sum(inside)))
}
b <- clean_points(burglary_raw, "Residential burglary records")
s <- clean_points(victims_raw, "Shooting-victim records")
burglary <- b$data
victims <- s$data
stopifnot(nrow(burglary) > 0, nrow(victims) > 0)

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 5: Transform features

5A: Inspect skew and curvature


Show code
tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>%
  transmute(`Burglary density` = burglary_per_sqmi,

title: Building Features: Predicting Philadelphia Commute Times
text:
Part 6: Final model

Combine useful features, then compare
Starting with the baseline, I consider the better count/raw-density/log-density version of burglary, victim density, nearest-victim distance, and the better linear/quadratic/categorical City Hall measure, in that order. I attempt a feature only when its individual candidate beats baseline and retain it in the combination only if it improves the current score. Every attempted combination is logged. This is a small search, not exhaustive subset selection. I choose the lowest RMSE among all evaluated candidates; ties favor the earlier specification.


Show code
best_id <- function(ids) {
  z <- model_log %>% filter(model %in% ids)
  z$model[which.min(z$cv_rmse)]
}
candidate_groups <- list(c("m2", "m3", "m7"), "m4", "m5", c("m6", "m8", "m9"))
current_id <- "m1"
baseline_terms <- attr(terms(f1), "term.labels")
for (i in seq_along(candidate_groups)) {
  id <- best_id(candidate_groups[[i]])
  if (model_log$cv_rmse[match(id, model_log$model)] >= model_log$cv_rmse[1]) next
  extra_terms <- setdiff(attr(terms(formulas[[id]]), "term.labels"), baseline_terms)
  combined <- reformulate(unique(c(attr(terms(formulas[[current_id]]), "term.labels"),
                                    extra_terms)), response = "y")
  combined_id <- paste0("combine", i)
  log_model(combined_id, combined, paste("Add", model_log$added[match(id, model_log$model)]),
            current_id, "Retain only if CV RMSE decreases")
  if (tail(model_log$improvement, 1) > 0) current_id <- combined_id
}
selected_id <- model_log$model[which.min(model_log$cv_rmse)]
f_final <- formulas[[selected_id]]
m_final <- lm(f_final, data = tracts)
final_rmse <- model_log$cv_rmse[match(selected_id, model_log$model)]
baseline_rmse <- model_log$cv_rmse[1]
model_log <- model_log %>% add_row(model = "final", added = paste("Selected", selected_id),
  compared_to = "m1", cv_rmse = final_rmse, improvement = baseline_rmse - final_rmse,
  notes = "Reuse selected candidate's score; no independent test set")
summary(m_final)

The selected model is m8: y ~ income_k + ba_share + renter_share + pop_density_k + dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2). Its mean fold RMSE is 4.99 minutes, compared with 5.14 for baseline, a 2.9% reduction. The rank correlation between ACS CV and absolute held-out error is 0.17, a weak positive association. The upward smooth and the low-reliability group’s larger mean error support some connection to sampling uncertainty, but large misses also occur at moderate CVs. Only one tract is classified High, so that group’s average is not a stable comparison. The median approximate outcome standard error is 7.01 minutes, exceeding final model RMSE of 4.99 minutes. This does not mean sampling noise explains more than 100% of the error: the ratio-MOE approximation omits covariance, and a median estimated SE is not a decomposition of prediction error. Omitted variables, predictor error, and model misspecification also contribute.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

text:
Part 0: Setup


Code
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(caret)

Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""   # should print TRUE


[1] TRUE



The cross-validation helper
This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.


Code
ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}




The model log
Every time you fit a new model, add a row. By the end, this table is the story of your assignment.


Code
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
)

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?
url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=csv&q=",
              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n
                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))
read_csv(url)

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))

summary(tracts$n_burglary)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  0.000   4.000   7.000   9.458  13.000  48.000 


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)   # always inside the tract, unlike a centroid

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, stations)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
    st_distance(tract_pts, stations[nearest_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)




4D: Measuring distance to one place
Sometimes the “thing” is a single location, such as City Hall as a stand-in for the center of the regional economy.


Code
city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(tract_pts, city_hall)) / 5280)




4E: Your turn
Build at least three spatial features from your own layers, and use at least two types (count, density, nearest distance, distance to a place). After each one, fit a model, cross-validate it, and log it.


Code
# Feature 1: count burglaries in each tract
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., layer1)))
f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + n_burglary)
m2 <- lm(f2, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m2", added = "burglary count", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f2, tracts),
          notes = "Adds 2023 residential burglary count")

# Feature 2: normalize count by tract area
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(area_sqmi = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,
                            burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi)
f3 <- update(f2, . ~ . + burglary_per_sqmi)
m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m3", added = "burglaries per square mile", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts),
          notes = "Adds area-normalized 2023 burglary count")

# Feature 3: distance to nearest Indego station
tract_pts <- st_point_on_surface(tracts)
nearest_station_idx <- st_nearest_feature(tract_pts, layer2)
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(dist_station_mi = as.numeric(
  st_distance(tract_pts, layer2[nearest_station_idx, ], by_element = TRUE)) / 5280)
f4 <- update(f3, . ~ . + dist_station_mi)
m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m4", added = "distance to nearest Indego station", cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts),
          notes = "Adds nearest-station distance in miles")
model_log


# A tibble: 4 × 4
  model added                              cv_rmse notes                        
  <chr> <chr>                                <dbl> <chr>                        
1 m1    ACS baseline                          5.13 Mean commute minutes from AC…
2 m2    burglary count                        5.14 Adds 2023 residential burgla…
3 m3    burglaries per square mile            5.16 Adds area-normalized 2023 bu…
4 m4    distance to nearest Indego station    5.17 Adds nearest-station distanc…


Answer: Which spatial feature helped most? Did any feature you expected to help do nothing, or make CV RMSE worse? Why might that be?
Your answer:
Among the spatial additions, burglary count has the lowest CV RMSE (5.14 minutes). Compared with the baseline, the spatial model(s) that made CV RMSE worse are m2, m3, m4. Burglary may add only an indirect signal about commuting, and Indego distance does not measure SEPTA service or job destinations, so either could add little or even increase CV error.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()















Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)
summary(m_sq)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-18.5194  -3.0884  -0.0491   2.9256  16.3693 

Coefficients:
                Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)     25.87577    0.69995  36.968  < 2e-16 ***
dist_ch_mi       2.10433    0.25419   8.279 2.19e-15 ***
I(dist_ch_mi^2) -0.12422    0.01908  -6.511 2.39e-10 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.054 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1911,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1868 
F-statistic: 44.54 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()











5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )

tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


   ring   n
1  Core  79
2 Inner 134
3 Outer 167


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)
summary(m_cat)



Call:
lm(formula = y ~ ring, data = tracts)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-17.5146  -3.2886  -0.1537   3.1284  17.1430 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  27.5537     0.5699  48.349  < 2e-16 ***
ringInner     4.3575     0.7185   6.065 3.21e-09 ***
ringOuter     6.4529     0.6917   9.329  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.065 on 377 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.1876,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1833 
F-statistic: 43.52 on 2 and 377 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.




5D: Your turn
Try at least one of each: a log, a squared term, and a categorical variable. Choose which variables to transform based on your plots, not at random. Log each model.


Code
# Log transform skewed median household income
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(log_income = log1p(median_incomeE))
f_log <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + log_income)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m5", added = "log of median household income",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_log, tracts), notes = "Replaces raw income with log1p(income)")

# Allow the station-distance relationship to curve
f_sq <- update(f4, . ~ . + I(dist_station_mi^2))
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m6", added = "squared distance to Indego station",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_sq, tracts), notes = "Tests a curved station-distance relationship")

# Compare income quartiles as categories
tracts <- tracts %>% mutate(income_group = factor(dplyr::ntile(median_incomeE, 4),
  levels = 1:4, labels = c("Q1_lowest", "Q2", "Q3", "Q4_highest")))
f_cat <- update(f4, . ~ . - median_incomeE + income_group)
m_cat <- lm(f_cat, data = tracts)
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "m7", added = "income quartile factor",
          cv_rmse = cv_rmse(f_cat, tracts), notes = "Replaces linear income with four income groups")
model_log


# A tibble: 7 × 4
  model added                              cv_rmse notes                        
  <chr> <chr>                                <dbl> <chr>                        
1 m1    ACS baseline                          5.13 Mean commute minutes from AC…
2 m2    burglary count                        5.14 Adds 2023 residential burgla…
3 m3    burglaries per square mile            5.16 Adds area-normalized 2023 bu…
4 m4    distance to nearest Indego station    5.17 Adds nearest-station distanc…
5 m5    log of median household income        5.18 Replaces raw income with log…
6 m6    squared distance to Indego station    5.12 Tests a curved station-dista…
7 m7    income quartile factor                5.16 Replaces linear income with …


Answer: Which transformation helped most? For your categorical variable, write one sentence reading one of its coefficients correctly, naming the reference level.
Your answer:
The transformation with the lowest CV RMSE is squared distance to Indego station (5.12 minutes). In the categorical model, Q1_lowest is the reference group: holding the other predictors in that model constant, Q4_highest tracts are predicted to have 1.5 minutes shorter mean commutes than Q1_lowest tracts.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
What’s still missing? Look at your final residual map. Name one thing about those places you’d want to measure next, and where you might get the data.
How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer:
The best tested addition is squared distance to Indego station; the weakest is log of median household income. Their CV RMSEs are 5.12 and 5.18 minutes; CV error on unseen tracts is the basis for choosing features. In the final model, a one-percentage-point increase in bachelor’s-or-higher share changes predicted commute time by -0.07 minutes, holding other predictors constant. For tract GEOID 42101034701, with bachelor’s share closest to the sample median, the final model predicts 34.51 minutes.
The residual map and the feature comparisons suggest where the model needs more information. A useful next measure would be transit travel time and service frequency to job centers, using SEPTA schedules and Census LEHD/LODES job locations. Burglary is only an indirect measure of neighborhood context, and station distance does not capture routes, transfers, or frequency, so those spatial features can help little even when the underlying idea matters. The correlation between ACS outcome CV and absolute final residual is 0.28. A positive association means larger misses tend to occur where the ACS outcome is less reliable; it would suggest uncertainty contributes to the error, but it would not establish that uncertainty explains all of it. I would also compare the residual map with the reliability plot, since places with reliable ACS estimates can still have large prediction errors when the model omits important local conditions. The log-income model tests whether income has diminishing returns, the squared-distance model allows the station relationship to bend, and the income-group model allows step changes between quartiles. Whichever gives the smallest held-out error earns its place as a predictive feature, even if its coefficient is not statistically significant. These comparisons describe predictive association across tracts, not the causal effect of changing income, education, or infrastructure.

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
This is not a competition. There’s no leaderboard and no target RMSE. The goal is to practice the full prediction workflow on a question you choose, and to find out what actually helps. Some features you’re sure will help won’t, and some you add on a whim will. Both are findings.
You’ll:

Choose a tract-level outcome for Philadelphia and check whether it’s reliable enough to model (Weeks 2–3).
Fit a baseline model and cross-validate it (Week 5).
Pull data from Philadelphia’s open data portal through its API and build spatial features: counts, densities, and distances (Week 4, plus one new tool).
Transform variables with logs, squared terms, and categories. Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before Part 5.
Keep a model log the whole way through, and compare where your first and final models go wrong.

Timing. Parts 1–4 use only what we’ve covered through Week 5. You can finish them before the October 9 lecture. Part 5 is new material; the lecture explains it, and the instructions below give you the essentials.
Type the code yourself. The worked examples show the pattern. Your job is to apply it to your outcome and your data choices.








Important1. Don’t drop rows



Every model is cross-validated on the same tracts with the same folds, so the rows in your model log are comparable. If a new variable has missing values, fill them (for example, 0 for a count, or the median with a note) or choose a different variable. The cv_rmse() helper below will stop and tell you if you break this rule.


Your outcome comes from the 2019–2023 ACS. Pull open data from 2023 or earlier (2021–2023 is ideal). Using 2025 data to predict a 2023 outcome uses information from the future, which a real prediction model would never have.



Don’t use any variable that’s built from your outcome or measures the same thing another way. Ask yourself: would an agency trying to predict this outcome for a tract have this variable? If the answer is “only because it’s basically the outcome,” leave it out.

section: Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
text:
Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}



Finding a table name
On a dataset’s OpenDataPhilly page, look for the API link. The table name is the word after FROM in the example query. To see what values a column takes before you filter on it, ask for a count in CSV format:


Code
# What kinds of crime are in the incidents table in 2023?

              URLencode("SELECT text_general_code, COUNT(*) AS n
                         FROM incidents_part1_part2
                         WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2024-01-01'
                         GROUP BY text_general_code ORDER BY n DESC"))
read_csv(url)

Part 4: Building spatial features
Every feature below reuses a Week 4 tool. The worked examples use burglaries and Indego stations; you build the same types from your own layers.

4A: Counting
How many burglaries fall in each tract?


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(n_burglary = lengths(st_intersects(., burglary)))


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
summary(tracts$n_burglary)


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


A tract with no burglaries gets 0, not NA, so Rule 1 is safe.


4B: Density: don’t skip this
Raw counts mostly measure tract size. A big tract has more of everything. Normalize by area, by population, or by housing units, depending on what makes sense for the thing you’re counting.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    area_sqmi         = as.numeric(st_area(.)) / 27878400,   # sq ft in a sq mile
    burglary_per_sqmi = n_burglary / area_sqmi,
    burglary_per_1k   = n_burglary / total_popE * 1000
  )


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found








NotePer capita in low-population tracts



If a tract has 40 residents and 3 burglaries, its rate is 75 per 1,000, which is a huge number built on tiny counts. Look at the tracts with the highest per-capita rates before you trust them. This is the Week 3 lesson about small denominators again.




4C: Measuring distance to the nearest thing
How far is each tract from its nearest Indego station? Use the Week 4 pattern: find the nearest feature, then measure to it element by element.


Code
stations <- st_read("https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/", quiet = TRUE) %>%
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

title: Assignment: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = log1p(burglary_per_sqmi))) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found








Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.


Code
m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
summary(m_sq)


Error:
! object 'm_sq' not found


Reading the coefficient: you can’t read either coefficient alone anymore. The effect of X depends on where you are along X. A positive linear term with a negative squared term means Y rises with X and then levels off or turns down. Plot the fitted curve to see it:


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = dist_ch_mi, y = y)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x + I(x^2), se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  theme_minimal()


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found




5C: Categorical variables
Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.


Code
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer"))
  )


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
tracts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(ring)


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
m_cat <- lm(y ~ ring, data = tracts)


Error:
! object 'tracts' not found


Code
summary(m_cat)


Error:
! object 'm_cat' not found


Reading the coefficients: R turns a factor with k categories into k − 1 dummy variables. The category left out is the reference level (here, “Core,” the first level). Each coefficient is the difference from the reference: ringOuter is how much higher or lower predicted Y is in outer tracts compared to core tracts, holding everything else in the model constant. To change the reference, use relevel(ring, ref = "Outer").






NoteCheck your group sizes



If a category has only a handful of tracts, its coefficient is unstable, and in cross-validation some folds may not contain it at all. Aim for at least 20 tracts per category.
