title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
R Data Basics

Objects, functions, and packages

An object stores a value or result. Use <- (or =) to assign a value to an object.
A function performs an operation. Its inputs are called arguments.
A package adds functions to R. Install a package once; load it with library() in each new R session where you need it.
The console is useful for trying code, but its history is not a durable record. Save reusable work in an .R script or a .qmd document.
In a Quarto document, R code goes in a code chunk and can run when the document is rendered.


# Install a package once, if needed:
# install.packages("dplyr")

library(dplyr)



Data frames and tibbles
A data frame is a table: rows are observations and columns are variables. A tibble is a modern data frame that prints more readably and behaves consistently in tidyverse workflows. R is case-sensitive, so Name, name, and NAME are different names.



Name
Income
MOE




Adams
78,975
3,334


Berks
74,617
1,191


Bucks
104,200
1,502

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Core dplyr Verbs
The usual pattern is to take a table, apply a verb, and get a table back.








Verb
What it does
Example




filter()
Keeps rows that meet a condition
filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)


select()
Keeps or reorders columns
select(counties, Name, moe_pct)


mutate()
Adds or changes a computed column
mutate(counties, income_thousands = Income / 1000)


arrange()
Sorts rows; use desc() for descending order
arrange(counties, desc(moe_pct))


group_by() + summarize()
Calculates summaries for each group
group_by(data, State) |> summarize(min_income = min(Income))



For example, summarize income by state:

county_example <- tibble::tibble(
  County = c("Orange", "Nassau", "Orange", "Sacramento"),
  State = c("NY", "NY", "CA", "CA"),
  Income = c(70000, 80000, 90000, 100000)
)

county_example |>
  group_by(State) |>
  summarize(min_income = min(Income), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  State min_income
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 CA         90000
2 NY         70000


The result has one row per state: NY has a minimum income of 70,000, and CA has a minimum income of 90,000.

Combining steps with a pipe
A pipe (|> or %>%) passes the result from one step into the next. Read the steps as “and then.” The base R pipe |> is available in recent versions of R; %>% is provided by packages such as dplyr.

new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(Name, moe_pct)

This keeps counties where moe_pct is above 10, sorts them from highest to lowest, and returns only the Name and moe_pct columns. Without a pipe, these can be written as separate intermediate steps:

step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, Name, moe_pct)

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Census and ACS Data

Decennial Census and American Community Survey

The Decennial Census counts the population every 10 years. Historically, its long form collected more detailed information; detailed demographic and socioeconomic estimates are now primarily collected through the ACS.
The American Community Survey (ACS) is an ongoing sample survey. Estimates describe a population; they are not a complete count of every household.
ACS 1-year estimates are more current and are generally published for areas with populations of at least 65,000.
ACS 5-year estimates pool 60 months of survey data and are available for smaller geographies, including census tracts and block groups. A label such as “2016 ACS 5-year” refers to the 2012–2016 data period, not a single-year snapshot.
The ACS 3-year product was discontinued after the 2011–2013 release.

ACS estimates are published with a margin of error (MOE). An estimate is commonly read as an interval from estimate - MOE to estimate + MOE. ACS MOEs are reported at a 90% confidence level. A larger MOE relative to the estimate means less precision. Be careful when comparing or combining estimates, especially for small areas or subgroups.
If a percentage MOE column is needed, one common calculation is 100 * MOE / estimate. Confirm the definition used by the dataset before interpreting it. For the table above, that formula gives about 4.2% for Adams, 1.6% for Berks, and 1.4% for Bucks; these are not the same as the shorthand moe_pct values in the class notes.


Census table IDs and estimate columns
An ACS table ID such as B19013_001E can be read as:

B: detailed base table (as opposed to a subject table such as S1901).
19013: table number; B19013 is median household income.
001: line within the table.
E: estimate. The corresponding M suffix identifies the margin of error, as in B19013_001M.



Geographic levels and GEOIDs
Census data can be requested at different geographic levels, such as state, county, tract, block group, and (for decennial Census data) block. A census tract is a neighborhood-scale statistical area, often containing roughly 1,200–8,000 people, with a target near 4,000. A tract is only an approximate proxy for a neighborhood. Block groups are smaller and often have higher MOEs because their samples are smaller; blocks are the smallest Census geography and generally do not have ACS estimates. Boundaries can change between censuses, which complicates comparisons over time. Longitudinal crosswalks and projects such as NHGIS and LTDB can help with historical comparisons.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier. Store GEOIDs as character strings so leading zeros are preserved. For a census tract, the 11-digit GEOID is made from the 2-digit state FIPS code, 3-digit county FIPS code, and 6-digit tract code. For example, 42101000100 consists of state 42, county 101, and tract 000100.


Requesting ACS data with tidycensus
get_acs() from the tidycensus package requests Census estimates. You need a Census API key configured for the package. This example requests two ACS 5-year variables for Pennsylvania counties:

# Install once if needed, then load in each R session:
# install.packages("tidycensus")
library(tidycensus)

# Look up available codes and labels:
acs_variables <- load_variables(year = 2023, dataset = "acs5")

# Request selected variables:
pa_county_acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001", "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)

The default output is long: each geography-variable combination has a row, with columns such as GEOID, NAME, variable, estimate, and moe. The values below are a schematic example based on the class notes, not a promise of the exact result for every ACS year.



GEOID
NAME
variable
estimate
moe




42001
Adams County, Pennsylvania
B19013_001
78,975
3,334


42001
Adams County, Pennsylvania
B01003_001
102,311
NA



In a long table, one column identifies which variable each row represents. Use output = "wide" when you prefer one row per geography and separate estimate/MOE columns for each requested variable:

pa_county_acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001", "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

In wide output, GEOID and NAME identify the county, and each variable has estimate and MOE columns (for example, B19013_001E and B19013_001M). Long and wide formats contain the same information arranged differently.

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Key Takeaways

Use filter() for rows, select() for columns, mutate() for computed columns, and arrange() for sorting.
Use group_by() with summarize() to reduce many observations to one summary row per group.
Pipes make a sequence of data transformations easier to read.
ACS figures are estimates with uncertainty. Read the MOE alongside each estimate and note the survey period and geographic level.
Keep GEOIDs as strings so leading zeros are not lost.

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
R Basics

Where does code go?

Console → try a quick command; it is not saved as a note.
R script (.R) → save code so you can use it again.
Quarto (.qmd) → put words, code, tables, and pictures together.
Code chunk → a box of R code inside a Quarto note.



How to read a line of code
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000)

result → the name of the new object (a place to keep the answer).
<- → “put the answer into.” = can also assign a value.
filter() → the function (the action).
counties → the table to work on.
population > 50000 → the rule for keeping rows.
R cares about capital letters: Name, name, and NAME are different.



Packages: tools for R

A package adds extra tools to R.
Install a package once; load it each time you start a new R session.

# Do this once, if dplyr is not installed:
# install.packages("dplyr")

# Do this in a session when you need dplyr:
library(dplyr)


Tables: data frames and tibbles

A table has rows and columns.
A row is one thing being described, such as one county.
A column is one fact about it, such as its name or income.
A data frame is an R table.
A tibble is a data frame that prints in a tidier way.

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
dplyr: Actions for Tables
Think of each verb as a small instruction for a table:

filter() → keep certain rows.

Example: filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)

select() → keep certain columns.

Example: select(counties, Name, moe_pct)

mutate() → add or change a column.

Example: mutate(counties, income_thousands = Income / 1000)

arrange() → put rows in a new order.

Example: arrange(counties, desc(moe_pct)) sorts biggest to smallest.

group_by() → make piles of rows with the same label.
summarize() → make one short answer for each pile.


Example: smallest income in each state

library(dplyr)

county_example <- tibble::tibble(
  County = c("Orange", "Nassau", "Orange", "Sacramento"),
  State = c("NY", "NY", "CA", "CA"),
  Income = c(70000, 80000, 90000, 100000)
)

county_example |>
  group_by(State) |>
  summarize(min_income = min(Income), .groups = "drop")

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  State min_income
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 CA         90000
2 NY         70000



The table is split into NY and CA piles.
R finds the smallest income in each pile.
NY answer → 70,000.
CA answer → 90,000.



Pipes: “and then”

A pipe sends one answer to the next step.
|> is R’s pipe; %>% is another pipe used by tidyverse packages.

counties
  |> filter(moe_pct > 10)       # and then keep rows above 10
  |> arrange(desc(moe_pct))     # and then sort biggest first
  |> select(Name, moe_pct)      # and then keep these two columns
All counties → filter → sort → select → smaller, ordered table

This example uses a table named counties from class, so it is a practice pattern.
Without pipes, save each step in a new object:

step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, Name, moe_pct)

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Census Data: Counts and Estimates

Two ways to learn about people

Decennial Census

Counts the population every 10 years.
The old Census long form asked extra questions; today the ACS collects most detailed community information.

American Community Survey (ACS)

Asks a sample of households questions over time.
Uses the answers to estimate facts about the whole population.
An estimate is not an exact count of every household.




ACS time periods

1-year ACS

Newer information.
Usually available for places with at least 65,000 people.

5-year ACS

Combines 5 years of survey answers.
Available for smaller places, including tracts and block groups.
“2016 ACS 5-year” uses data from 2012–2016.

3-year ACS

Discontinued after the 2011–2013 release.




Estimate and margin of error (MOE)

Estimate → the survey’s best estimate.
MOE → the “wiggle room” around that estimate.
A simple way to picture the range:

estimate − MOE  ← likely range →  estimate + MOE

ACS MOEs use a 90% confidence level.
Bigger MOE compared with the estimate → less precise result.
Small places often have bigger MOEs because fewer people answer the survey.
Keep the estimate and MOE together when you report a result.
One common relative-MOE calculation is 100 × MOE / estimate.

Example: Adams, 3,334 / 78,975 × 100 ≈ 4.2%.
The shorthand moe_pct values in the class table do not match this formula, so check how that column was made before using it.




Census table codes
Example code: B19013_001E

B → detailed base table.
19013 → table number; B19013 is median household income.
001 → line in the table.
E → estimate.
M → margin of error; for example, B19013_001M.

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Places and GEOIDs

Geography gets smaller
State → County → Census tract → Block group → Block
large place                                  small place

A census tract is a small area used to organize Census data.

Often about 1,200–8,000 people; target is near 4,000.
It can be a rough neighborhood stand-in, but is not always a real neighborhood.

A block group is smaller than a tract; small samples can mean larger MOEs.
A block is the smallest Census area.

Blocks are used in the Decennial Census; ACS estimates generally are not available at block level.

Boundaries can change over time, making comparisons tricky.

NHGIS and LTDB offer tools for comparing areas across years.




GEOID: an ID for a place

Keep a GEOID as text, not a number, so starting zeros stay there.
An 11-character tract GEOID is built from three parts:

42 | 101 | 000100
state  county  tract
              ↓
       42101000100

42 → Pennsylvania state code.
101 → county code.
000100 → tract code.

title: Week 2: Tibbles, dplyr, and Census Data
text:
Getting ACS Data with tidycensus

load_variables() → look up variable codes and labels (like a codebook).
get_acs() → ask for ACS estimates.
A Census API key must be set up for tidycensus to download data.
This practice example asks for median income and population in Pennsylvania counties:


# Install once if needed:
# install.packages("tidycensus")
library(tidycensus)

# Look up the codes and labels:
acs_variables <- load_variables(year = 2023, dataset = "acs5")

# Download the estimates:
pa_county_acs <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001", "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)


Long and wide tables

Long → one row for each place-and-variable pair.

A variable column says which fact is in that row.

Wide → one row for each place; each fact gets its own columns.
Same information, arranged differently:

LONG                         WIDE
County | variable | estimate County | income | population
Adams  | income   | ...      Adams  | ...    | ...
Adams  | population | ...

get_acs() returns long data by default.
To ask for wide data, add output = "wide":

pa_county_acs_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c("B19013_001", "B01003_001"),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

Each variable has an estimate column (E) and an MOE column (M).
The class example below is only a practice illustration; check actual output for the year you request.




GEOID
County
Variable
Estimate
MOE




42001
Adams
B19013_001
78,975
3,334


42001
Adams
B01003_001
102,311
NA in class note

text:
Remember These

filter() picks rows; select() picks columns.
mutate() makes a column; arrange() sorts rows.
group_by() makes groups; summarize() makes a short answer for each group.
Pipes mean “and then.”
ACS values are estimates, so read the MOE too.
A 5-year ACS number covers 5 years.
GEOIDs are text and tell you which place a row describes.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Ask a question → choose a graph → show the data → show how wiggly the answer is
This week we learned how to make graphs with ggplot2 and how to read estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS). A graph helps us see patterns. An uncertainty measure helps us remember that a survey estimate is not a perfect count.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Ask a question → choose a graph → show the data → show how wiggly the answer is
This week we learned how to make graphs with ggplot2 and how to read estimates from the American Community Survey (ACS). A graph helps us see patterns. An uncertainty measure helps us remember that a survey estimate is not a perfect count.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Why Pictures Help

Anscombe’s Quartet
Anscombe’s Quartet is four small sets of numbers. The sets have almost the same averages, correlations, and fitted lines. But when we draw them, they look very different.
Same-looking summary numbers ≠ same-looking data
One set might make a curve, another might have a far-away point, and another might make a neat line. A few summary numbers can hide these surprises. Draw the data before deciding what it means.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Build a Graph with ggplot2
Think of a graph as a picture made from a few parts:

Data → the table you want to draw.
Aesthetics → which columns control position, color, or size.
Geometry → the kind of marks to draw, such as dots or bars.

Download library first
install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidycensus", "gt"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(gt)

ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x = population, y = estimate) +
  geom_point()
Read it like a recipe:

ggplot(my_data) picks the table and opens a blank canvas.
aes(...) maps columns to parts of the picture.
geom_point() draws dots.

Use the real name of your table in place of my_data.

Map columns to the picture
For example, we could show:



Column in the data
Part of the picture




population
Left-to-right position (x-axis)


estimate
Up-and-down position (y-axis)


reliability
Color


moe
Size or an error bar



A graph can show several facts at once. For example, each dot can show a place’s population, estimate, and reliability.


Map a column or choose one color?
Put a column inside aes() when it should control a visual feature:

ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x = population, y = estimate, color = reliability) +
  geom_point()
Now the dots get different colors depending on their reliability value.
Put a fixed choice outside aes() when every mark should look the same:
#| eval: false
ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x = population, y = estimate) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")
Here every dot is blue. The word "blue" is not a column in the table; it is a style choice.
Inside aes()  → a column from the data chooses the look
Outside aes() → you choose one look for every mark

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
section: Pick a Graph That Answers Your Question
text:
Pick a Graph That Answers Your Question



What do I want to see?
Try this




How one number is spread out
geom_histogram()


How two numbers go together
geom_point()


How groups compare
geom_boxplot() or geom_col()


How something changes over time
geom_line()


How much wiggle room an estimate has
geom_errorbar()



A histogram groups numbers into bins, like sorting blocks by height. A scatterplot uses dots to show two numbers together. A boxplot gives a quick picture of how values differ across groups. A line graph connects values in time order.

Show groups in separate panels
A facet makes a small panel for each group. For example, this makes one panel for each reliability label:
#| eval: false
ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x = population, y = estimate) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~reliability)
This can make groups easier to compare. Facets arrange the data; they do not change the data itself.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
ACS Estimates Have Wiggle Room
The ACS asks a sample of people questions and uses their answers to estimate things about a larger population. So an ACS number is an estimate, not an exact count of every person.

Estimate → the survey’s best guess.
Margin of error (MOE) → a range of wiggle room around that guess.
Standard error (SE) → another way to measure how much the estimate might wobble.

A simple picture is:
estimate − MOE  ← possible range →  estimate + MOE
ACS margins of error usually use a 90% confidence level. For that level:
MOE = 1.645 × SE
SE  = MOE ÷ 1.645
Example: If an estimate is $45,000 and its MOE is $8,000, then its SE is about $8,000 ÷ 1.645 = $4,863.

Draw the wiggle room
An error bar stretches from the estimate minus the MOE to the estimate plus the MOE:
#| eval: false
ggplot(my_data) +
  aes(x = place, y = estimate) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = estimate - moe,
                    ymax = estimate + moe))
The dot is the estimate. The line is the wiggle room. Two dots can look different even when their long error bars overlap, so check the uncertainty too.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
How Reliable Is an Estimate?
The coefficient of variation (CV) compares the wiggle room to the size of the estimate. It is useful because an MOE of 100 may be small for an estimate of 10,000 but large for an estimate of 200.
CV = (SE ÷ estimate) × 100
   = (MOE ÷ 1.645 ÷ estimate) × 100

Lower CV → less uncertainty compared with the estimate.
Higher CV → more uncertainty compared with the estimate.

Class notes use these rough guideposts: below 15% is low sampling error, 15–30% is medium, and above 30% is high. A class exercise or project may use different cutoffs, so follow the rule it gives you. These are helpful labels, not magic lines that make an estimate suddenly good or bad.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
New Calculations Need New Uncertainty
If we use survey estimates to calculate a new answer, that answer also has uncertainty. We need to carry the wiggle room along.

moe_sum() → helps find the MOE when we add estimates.
moe_prop() → helps find the MOE when one count is part of another, such as people in poverty out of all people.
moe_ratio() → helps find the MOE for a ratio when the top count is not part of the bottom count.

A poverty rate is a proportion because the people in poverty are part of the total population:
poverty rate = people in poverty ÷ total population
Do not just add MOEs together when adding estimates. Use the matching uncertainty function. If you turn a proportion into a percent by multiplying by 100, multiply its MOE by 100 too.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Compare ACS Numbers Over Time
ACS 5-year estimates cover five years at once. That means nearby periods can overlap:
2018–2022
   2019–2023  ← shares four years with the first period
A cleaner comparison uses periods that do not overlap, such as 2014–2018 and 2019–2023. When comparing dollar amounts across years, remember that prices change; adjust income for inflation before explaining what the difference means.

Example: Did income really go up?
Suppose the estimates are:



Period
Estimate
MOE




2014–2018
$45,000
$8,000


2019–2023
$62,000
$11,000



The difference is $62,000 − $45,000 = $17,000. But both estimates have wiggle room. We need to check the wiggle room around the difference too.
First find each standard error, then combine them:
SE₁ = 8,000 ÷ 1.645  ≈ 4,863
SE₂ = 11,000 ÷ 1.645 ≈ 6,687

SE of the difference = √(SE₁² + SE₂²) ≈ 8,268
For a 90% confidence interval around the change, multiply by 1.645:
change ± (1.645 × SE of the difference)
$17,000 ± $13,601
about $3,399 to $30,601
This range stays above zero, so these estimates give evidence of an increase at the 90% level, using this method. If a change’s range crosses zero, the data do not clearly tell us whether it went up, went down, or stayed about the same. A difference between two estimates by itself does not prove a clear change.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
section: R Practice: New York County Data
text:
R Practice: New York County Data
The pages use New York county data about people living below the poverty level. get_acs() downloads estimates and MOEs. Here are small, non-running examples to show the pattern; the real pages include longer code and charts.
#| eval: false
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B17001_002", # people below the poverty level
  state = "NY",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5"
)
The result has columns such as GEOID (place ID), NAME (place name), estimate, and moe. We can add a relative MOE column and a simple label:
#| eval: false
county_data <- county_data |>
  mutate(
    moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
      moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )
This example uses MOE as a percent of the estimate, which is not the same as CV. For CV, first change MOE to SE by dividing by 1.645. Reliability labels and cutoffs depend on the rule chosen for a particular exercise.
We can then color the dots by reliability or show one panel per reliability group:
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data) +
  aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct, color = reliability) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~reliability)
For a long list of counties, a chart can get crowded. One helpful step is to sort places by MOE and show a smaller group. Another is to use coord_flip() so long place names are easier to read.

The Week 3 plots, step by step
The next pictures use New York county data from the example above. The code is shown so you can see how each picture was made. These pictures are the saved results from the linked Week 3 example page.
For the colored-dot plots, the example page labels counties using moe_pct: under 5% is high confidence, 5–10% is moderate, and 10% or more is low confidence. That is a different rule from the CV guideposts above, so always check which measure and cutoffs a graph uses.

1. Put two numbers on a scatterplot
Each dot is one county. The bottom axis shows the poverty estimate; the side axis shows its margin of error as a percent of the estimate.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point()



New York counties: poverty estimate on the x-axis and relative margin of error on the y-axis.




2. Let a data column choose the color
Here, each county’s reliability label chooses the dot’s color. The legend explains what the colors mean.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data, aes(
  x = estimate,
  y = moe_pct,
  color = reliability
)) +
  geom_point()



New York county dots colored by reliability category.




3. Choose one color for every dot
This time, "blue" is a style choice, so it goes outside aes(). It does not come from a data column.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point(color = "blue")



The same New York county dots, all colored blue.




4. Add an error bar to show wiggle room
The bar stretches from the estimate minus its MOE to the estimate plus its MOE. One bar is drawn for each county.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = NAME, y = estimate)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe)
  )



Poverty estimates for New York counties with margin-of-error bars.




5. Make a long chart easier to read
Showing every county at once can be crowded. This code keeps the 15 counties with the largest relative MOEs and turns the chart sideways so the names fit.
#| eval: false
top_15 <- county_data |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  mutate(NAME = stringr::str_remove(NAME, " County, New York"))

ggplot(top_15, aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = estimate - moe, ymax = estimate + moe),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  coord_flip()



The 15 New York counties with the largest relative margins of error, shown with poverty estimates and error bars.




6. Put each reliability group in its own panel
facet_wrap() makes one small graph for each reliability label. This can make the groups easier to compare.
#| eval: false
ggplot(county_data, aes(x = estimate, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~reliability) +
  theme_minimal()



Separate scatterplot panels for the New York county reliability categories.




7. Show which county estimates changed clearly
These bars compare poverty counts in two five-year periods that do not overlap. Each error bar shows uncertainty around the change. A bar that stays on one side of zero gives evidence of a change; one that crosses zero is less clear.
First, put both periods side by side and calculate the difference and its MOE:
#| eval: false
poverty_wide <- poverty_change |>
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, estimate, moe) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(estimate, moe)
  )

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide |>
  mutate(
    change = `estimate_2019-2023` - `estimate_2014-2018`,
    se_1 = `moe_2014-2018` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `moe_2019-2023` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = 1.645 * se_diff,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )
Then draw the counties whose changes are large compared with their wiggle room:
#| eval: false
poverty_tested |>
  filter(significant) |>
  mutate(NAME = stringr::str_remove(NAME, " County, New York")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change), y = change)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = change > 0)) +
  geom_errorbar(
    aes(ymin = change - moe_diff, ymax = change + moe_diff),
    width = 0.3
  ) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal()



Changes in New York county poverty counts between 2014–2018 and 2019–2023, with uncertainty bars.


The plot code uses a data table named poverty_change with one row per county and period. It can be made by running the get_poverty() recipe for 2018 and 2023, then stacking the two results with dplyr::bind_rows().



Save a little recipe as a function
An R function is a recipe we can use again. This example asks for the same kind of poverty estimate for whichever year we give it, then labels the five-year period:
#| eval: false
get_poverty <- function(year_end) {
  get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = "B17001_002",
    state = "NY",
    year = year_end,
    survey = "acs5"
  ) |>
    mutate(period = paste0(year_end - 4, "–", year_end))
}

# Ask the recipe for two different periods:
poverty_2018 <- get_poverty(2018) # 2014–2018
poverty_2023 <- get_poverty(2023) # 2019–2023
poverty_change <- dplyr::bind_rows(poverty_2018, poverty_2023)
Writing the function makes the recipe; it does not download anything yet. Calling it with 2018 or 2023 runs the recipe for that period.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Tiny Glossary



Word
Kid-friendly meaning




Data
The facts in your table


Estimate
The survey’s best guess


MOE
How far the guess might wiggle


SE
A measure of how much the guess might wobble


CV
Wiggle room compared with the size of the guess


aes()
The instructions that connect data columns to the picture


geom_*()
The kind of marks the graph draws


Facet
A little graph panel for each group

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change
text:
Remember These

Draw the data: matching averages do not guarantee matching patterns.
A ggplot is built from data, mappings, and a geometry.
Inside aes() means a data column controls a visual feature; outside means one fixed style.
Choose a graph that fits your question.
ACS numbers are estimates. Read the MOE too.
CV compares uncertainty with the size of the estimate.
Use the right moe_*() helper when calculating a new number.
Avoid overlapping ACS 5-year periods when comparing change.
Check the uncertainty around a difference; see whether its range includes zero.

title: Week 3: Visualizing Uncertainty and Change

Reflection

A picture can show patterns that averages hide.
Survey estimates have wiggle room, and we can show that wiggle room with numbers and graphs.
Before saying something changed, I should check whether the change is bigger than its uncertainty.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
This week connected the tables we have been using in R to the places they describe. We practiced joining tables by a shared identifier, adding geographic boundaries to ACS data, checking coordinate reference systems, and using spatial operations to study access to Indego stations in Philadelphia.
The lab asks: Which low-income tracts are farthest from a station, and how certain are their income estimates? To answer it, we need to define both “low-income” and “access.” Different definitions can produce different answers even when the underlying data is the same.
I used the lab and class recording to fill in these notes. The challenge section is for practice; it is not a record of what our team decided.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Using This File
The YAML settings show the code and its results. Maps appear below the chunks that create them. The page inherits its theme from _quarto.yml.

echo: true displays the code.
eval: true runs it during rendering.
output: true displays its output.
code-fold: false keeps code expanded.
freeze: false lets this page execute when the project is rendered.

The green Run button in RStudio runs a chunk while I am studying. A regular rendered HTML page displays the saved code and results; it does not provide a live R session in the browser.

Install packages once, load them each session
Run this installation command in the R Console if these packages are not already installed. This is a displayed example, not an executable installation chunk:
install.packages(
  c("tidyverse", "tidycensus", "sf"),
  repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
)
The following setup chunk does execute. Rendering starts its own R session, so packages and objects must be defined in this document rather than only in the Console.

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0
✔ ggplot2   4.0.3     ✔ tibble    3.3.1
✔ lubridate 1.9.5     ✔ tidyr     1.3.2
✔ purrr     1.2.2     
── Conflicts ────────────────────────────────────────── tidyverse_conflicts() ──
✖ dplyr::filter() masks stats::filter()
✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(tidycensus)
library(sf)

Linking to GEOS 3.14.1, GDAL 3.12.1, PROJ 9.7.1; sf_use_s2() is TRUE

# Displays only TRUE or FALSE, never the key itself.
Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") != ""

[1] TRUE


Keep the Census API key in .Renviron, not in this document. If I have not configured it, I can run tidycensus::census_api_key("MY_KEY", install = TRUE) privately in the Console using my actual key, then restart R. .Renviron should be excluded from Git.


Keep a local data snapshot
The first full render needs an internet connection, a working Census API key, and access to the Indego feed. The download chunks save their results to an RDS folder and reuse those files on later renders. This reduces repeated downloads and stops the live station layer from changing every time I correct a sentence.

data_dir <- "week04-data"
dir.create(data_dir, showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)

This folder is relative to the document’s execution directory. With Quarto’s usual file-based execution, it will be inside weekly-notes/. If the project sets execute-dir: project, it will be at the project root instead. RDS files preserve R objects, including their geometry and CRS. They are data snapshots, not API-key files.
To deliberately refresh a download, delete its corresponding RDS file and render again. Keep the files while studying if I want the same inputs each time. The code remains visible even when it reads a saved snapshot.

section: Joining Tables: Match by an Identifier
text:
Joining Tables: Match by an Identifier
A join combines information from two tables using a shared key. For Census tables, the key is often GEOID.

The example from class
These are small invented tables to make the joins easy to follow. The three-digit identifiers are teaching examples, not real tract GEOIDs.

income_23_example <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "300"),
  med_inc_23 = c(82000, 31500, 45000)
)

income_15_example <- tibble(
  GEOID = c("100", "200", "400"),
  med_inc_15 = c(61000, 27000, 39000)
)

income_23_example

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_23
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 100        82000
2 200        31500
3 300        45000

income_15_example

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 100        61000
2 200        27000
3 400        39000



left_join(income_23_example, income_15_example, by = "GEOID")

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA


The result is:



GEOID
med_inc_23
med_inc_15




100
82000
61000


200
31500
27000


300
45000
NA



The third identifier stays 300 because it came from the left table. It does not become 400. There is no 2015 match for 300, so its new income column contains NA. The 2015-only row for 400 is excluded.
Read left_join(x, y, by = "GEOID") as: keep the rows from x, find matching keys in y, and bring over their columns.


Reading the Venn diagram
The photograph from class illustrates table joins. Think of the circles as sets of identifiers. The shaded left circle includes identifiers with and without a match; the shared middle contains identifiers found in both tables; both circles together contain all identifiers.








Join
Rows kept
Identifiers in our example




left_join(x, y)
All left-table rows, with any matching right-table data
100, 200, 300


inner_join(x, y)
Rows with a match in both tables
100, 200


full_join(x, y)
Rows from both tables, including unmatched rows
100, 200, 300, 400


right_join(x, y)
All right-table rows, with any matching left-table data
100, 200, 400


anti_join(x, y)
Left-table rows with no match in the right table
300


semi_join(x, y)
Left-table rows that have a match; no new columns
100, 200




inner_join(income_23_example, income_15_example, by = "GEOID")

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000

full_join(income_23_example, income_15_example, by = "GEOID")

# A tibble: 4 × 3
  GEOID med_inc_23 med_inc_15
  <chr>      <dbl>      <dbl>
1 100        82000      61000
2 200        31500      27000
3 300        45000         NA
4 400           NA      39000

anti_join(income_23_example, income_15_example, by = "GEOID")

# A tibble: 1 × 2
  GEOID med_inc_23
  <chr>      <dbl>
1 300        45000


The circles are a memory aid, but real joins match rows, not just sets. If a key appears twice in the right table, one matching left row can become two output rows. A left join retains every left row, but it does not always retain the original row count. Swapping the inputs of a left join keeps the other table’s rows, which is why we often use a left join instead of switching to a right join. dplyr join reference


Why GEOIDs should be text
A tract GEOID has 11 characters: 2 for the state + 3 for the county + 6 for the tract. The tract part is six characters, not four. A block-group GEOID adds one more character. Census GEOID guide

example_geoid <- "06001400100"
nchar(example_geoid)

[1] 11

as.numeric(example_geoid)

[1] 6001400100


The numeric conversion drops the leading zero. A GEOID identifies a place; it is not a quantity to calculate with. Store it as character text and use compatible key types on both sides of a join. Changing a damaged number back with as.character() does not restore a missing zero automatically.
R is case-sensitive: GEOID, Geoid, and geoid are different names. Function names are also case-sensitive: use left_join(), not Left_join().

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Spatial Data: A Table Plus Geometry
text:
Spatial Data: A Table Plus Geometry
An sf object is a data frame with a special geometry column and spatial metadata. It can hold points, lines, polygons, or their multi-feature versions. The geometry records the coordinates; the other columns hold attributes such as income or population.

A bike-share station can be a POINT.
A street can be a LINESTRING.
A tract can be a POLYGON or MULTIPOLYGON.

A polygon needs a closed boundary made from several coordinates. A single coordinate pair is a point, not a complete polygon.
sf stands for simple features. It is an R package and an object representation. Shapefiles, GeoJSON, and GeoPackages are storage formats that sf can read or write; they are not the same thing as an sf object. Introduction to sf
Three related names appear in R: sf is the complete spatial table, sfc is its geometry list-column, and sfg represents one geometry. st_geometry(x) extracts the geometry, while st_drop_geometry(x) gives us the attributes without geometry. These are different operations.

Pull ACS data with boundaries

tract_file <- file.path(data_dir, "philly-tracts-acs2023.rds")

if (file.exists(tract_file)) {
  tracts_2023_all <- readRDS(tract_file)
} else {
  if (Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") == "") {
    stop("Configure CENSUS_API_KEY in .Renviron, restart R, and render again.")
  }

  tracts_2023_all <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(
      med_inc = "B19013_001",
      total_pop = "B01003_001"
    ),
    year = 2023,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide",
    geometry = TRUE,
    progress_bar = FALSE
  )

  saveRDS(tracts_2023_all, tract_file)
}

class(tracts_2023_all)

[1] "sf"         "data.frame"

glimpse(tracts_2023_all)

Rows: 408
Columns: 7
$ GEOID      <chr> "42101001500", "42101001800", "42101002802", "42101004001",…
$ NAME       <chr> "Census Tract 15; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania", "Cens…
$ med_incE   <dbl> 108378, 121719, 94427, 82258, 32997, 60817, 61621, 29122, 8…
$ med_incM   <dbl> 24143, 37496, 47914, 28135, 4045, 17642, 5502, 18512, 7973,…
$ total_popE <dbl> 3027, 3285, 5868, 4118, 4380, 1815, 3831, 2943, 4637, 5038,…
$ total_popM <dbl> 676, 345, 867, 456, 805, 202, 495, 785, 775, 830, 634, 868,…
$ geometry   <MULTIPOLYGON [°]> MULTIPOLYGON (((-75.16558 3..., MULTIPOLYGON (…


geometry = TRUE requests geographic boundaries along with the estimates. output = "wide" puts the variables side by side. The aliases create med_incE, med_incM, total_popE, and total_popM; E means estimate and M means margin of error.
The 2023 ACS five-year estimates describe 2019–2023, not only 2023. Median household income and total population also describe different universes: one summarizes household income, the other counts people. The available download arguments are documented in the tidycensus get_acs() reference.


Geometry is sticky
Selecting ordinary columns from an sf object normally retains its geometry. That is useful when mapping, but unnecessary for many tables.

  select(GEOID, med_incE) %>%
  head(3)

  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, med_incE) %>%
  head(3)

        GEOID med_incE
1 42101001500   108378

st_drop_geometry() returns an ordinary table. These pipelines do not change tracts_2023_all because we have not assigned their results back to that object. Removing geometry can reduce unnecessary work when summarizing attributes. sf and tidyverse methods

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Income Reliability and Our First Map
text:
Income Reliability and Our First Map
We retain tracts with a positive population estimate, as in the lab. We also keep the original unfiltered object for checking joins later.

philly_tracts <- tracts_2023_all %>%
  filter(total_popE > 0) %>%
  mutate(
    med_inc_se = if_else(
      !is.na(med_incM) & med_incM >= 0,
      med_incM / 1.645,
      NA_real_
    ),
    med_inc_cv = if_else(
      !is.na(med_incE) & med_incE > 0,
      med_inc_se / med_incE * 100,
      NA_real_
    ),
    reliability = case_when(
      is.na(med_inc_cv) ~ "Unavailable",
      med_inc_cv < 12 ~ "High",
      med_inc_cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE ~ "Low"
    )
  )

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(reliability)

  reliability   n
1        High 104
2         Low  23
3    Moderate 254
4 Unavailable  10


The ACS MOE is normally reported at the 90% confidence level, so we use the conversion in the Census accuracy worked examples:
[ SE = MOE / 1.645, CV = (SE / estimate). ]
These are the lab’s CV categories: below 12%, 12% through 40%, and above 40%. They are not the Week 2 categories based on moe_pct. CV and relative MOE differ by the factor 1.645. The labels summarize relative sampling uncertainty; they do not turn an estimate into a certainty.
The missing-value rule comes first so an unavailable CV does not fall through to “Low.” An undefined income estimate is not a zero-dollar income. Income with an invalid or unavailable MOE also cannot receive a numeric CV here.

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    retained_tracts = n(),
    missing_income = sum(is.na(med_incE)),
    unavailable_cv = sum(is.na(med_inc_cv))
  )

  retained_tracts missing_income unavailable_cv
1             391             10             10



ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = med_incE), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::dollar, na.value = "grey80") +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income, Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = "2019–2023 ACS five-year estimates",
    fill = "Income"
  )




Median household income estimates for populated Philadelphia tracts. Gray indicates a missing estimate.




geom_sf() reads the geometry column, so we do not need to map separate x and y columns. aes(fill = med_incE) maps income to interior color. color = NA removes polygon outlines. theme_void() changes presentation, not the data or CRS.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Joining 2015 Income to 2023 Tracts
This is a join diagnostic exercise. It is not yet a valid income-change analysis.

income15_file <- file.path(data_dir, "philly-income-acs2015.rds")

if (file.exists(income15_file)) {
  income_15 <- readRDS(income15_file)
} else {
  if (Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY") == "") {
    stop("Configure CENSUS_API_KEY before downloading the 2015 estimates.")
  }

  income_15 <- get_acs(
    geography = "tract",
    state = "PA",
    county = "Philadelphia",
    variables = c(med_inc_15 = "B19013_001"),
    year = 2015,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "wide",
    geometry = FALSE
  ) %>%
    select(GEOID, med_inc_15E, med_inc_15M)

  saveRDS(income_15, income15_file)
}

tibble(
  table = c("All 2023 tracts", "Populated 2023 tracts", "2015 tracts"),
  rows = c(nrow(tracts_2023_all), nrow(philly_tracts), nrow(income_15))
)

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  table                  rows
  <chr>                 <int>
1 All 2023 tracts         408
2 Populated 2023 tracts   391
3 2015 tracts             384



Check the keys, then join

stopifnot(
  is.character(philly_tracts$GEOID),
  is.character(income_15$GEOID),
  !anyDuplicated(philly_tracts$GEOID),
  !anyDuplicated(income_15$GEOID)
)

n_before_join <- nrow(philly_tracts)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(
    income_15 %>% mutate(in_2015 = TRUE),
    by = "GEOID"
  )

stopifnot(nrow(philly_tracts) == n_before_join)

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n(),
    no_2015_key_match = sum(is.na(in_2015)),
    matched_but_income_missing = sum(
      !is.na(in_2015) & is.na(med_inc_15E)
    )
  )

  n_tracts no_2015_key_match matched_but_income_missing
1      391                33                          2


stopifnot() stops execution if a check fails. anyDuplicated() returns zero when there are no duplicates. These checks help prevent an unexpected multiplication of rows.
The extra in_2015 column distinguishes two situations:

in_2015 is missing: the identifier did not match a row in the older table.
in_2015 is TRUE but income is missing: the row matched, but its estimate is unavailable.

Testing only is.na(med_inc_15E) would mix those situations together.

# Retained 2023 tracts with no 2015 key match.
philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(is.na(in_2015)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME) %>%
  head(10)

         GEOID                                                   NAME
1  42101020702 Census Tract 207.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
2  42101012502 Census Tract 125.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
3  42101013701 Census Tract 137.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
4  42101016002 Census Tract 160.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
5  42101036901 Census Tract 369.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
6  42101013702 Census Tract 137.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
7  42101000101   Census Tract 1.01; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
8  42101000404   Census Tract 4.04; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
9  42101000805   Census Tract 8.05; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania
10 42101000102   Census Tract 1.02; Philadelphia County; Pennsylvania

# Compare against ALL 2023 tracts, so the population filter does not
# make a still-existing tract look like a missing identifier.
income_15 %>%
  anti_join(st_drop_geometry(tracts_2023_all), by = "GEOID") %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 3
   GEOID       med_inc_15E med_inc_15M
   <chr>             <dbl>       <dbl>
 1 42101018800       21949        5375
 2 42101020700       51268        8987
 3 42101013700       35033        4377
 4 42101000100       92207       16328
 5 42101001300       81250       18169
 6 42101016000       45030        8727
 7 42101036900       47083       16973
 8 42101038300       21500        8025

10 42101004102       34102        4092




Why a successful join is not enough for change over time
Tracts can split, merge, or change boundaries between Census geography vintages. The 2015 and 2023 ACS products straddle the 2020 tract revisions. A missing match is a reason to investigate; even a matching GEOID does not prove that the geographic footprint stayed identical.
left_join() cannot resolve those boundary changes. A spatial join alone cannot resolve them either. Comparing the same places over time can require geographic relationship files or a documented harmonization method. We also need to express income in comparable inflation-adjusted dollars and account for uncertainty. Median incomes cannot simply be added or averaged to reconstruct a new tract’s median. Census geography relationship files

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems
A coordinate reference system, or CRS, explains what coordinates mean: their reference framework, axes, units, and, where applicable, projection. Numbers alone do not tell us whether a point is in Philadelphia, whether its units are feet, or whether its coordinates are longitude and latitude.

The geoid, ellipsoid, and datum
The recording includes the background behind these terms:

The geoid is a gravity-based reference surface approximating mean sea level, extended under the continents. It is not a model of every mountain and valley.
An ellipsoid is a smooth mathematical Earth model, slightly flattened at the poles. It gives us a manageable surface for coordinates.
A geodetic datum or reference frame connects that model and its coordinates to locations on Earth.
A geographic CRS adds a coordinate system, axes, and angular units to that reference framework. A datum alone is not the entire CRS.

The lowercase geoid in this discussion is completely different from the Census GEOID identifier. One is a reference surface; the other is a code in our data table. NOAA’s geoid explanation
The historical example from class was NAD27: it uses the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and a reference origin at Meades Ranch, Kansas. NAD83 uses GRS80 and was developed with a geocentric reference framework. The same numeric longitude and latitude can therefore refer to different ground positions under different datums. WGS84 is another widely used global reference system associated with GPS. NOAA’s datum FAQ
The practical lesson is to inspect the full CRS, not just check whether both layers use degrees. A datum mismatch can create a location offset even when two layers look almost aligned. The size of that offset depends on the systems and location; there is no universal correction to add by hand.


Geographic and projected coordinates









Family
Typical coordinates
Units
Main point




Geographic
Longitude and latitude
Degrees
Angular positions on an Earth model


Projected
Easting and northing
Often meters or feet
Planar coordinates designed for a region or purpose



A degree of longitude does not have the same ground length at every latitude. A buffer distance of 0.5 is therefore not automatically half a mile. For this lab, a local projected CRS makes distances and areas easier to interpret.
Geographic coordinates can still support geodesic distance calculations with appropriate software. The point is to understand the calculation and units, not to assume every operation in longitude and latitude is invalid.
In the common signed decimal-degree convention, longitude runs from -180 to 180 and latitude from -90 to 90. A Philadelphia coordinate near longitude -75 and latitude 40 is plausible. Those ranges are useful clues, not proof of a CRS. Confirm the metadata. In typical sf point construction, x is longitude and y is latitude when supplying longitude/latitude coordinates.


Projections preserve different properties
Common projection families include cylindrical, transverse cylindrical, conic, and azimuthal (planar). These describe how a projection is constructed. A separate question is what it preserves.
The class demonstration used an orange and a sheet of paper to explain flattening a curved surface. It is a useful analogy for distortion, although many projections are mathematical transformations rather than literal shadows from a light. Tangent and secant constructions help explain reference lines or points where scale is controlled. A projection works best in its intended region, not equally well everywhere.








Property
Meaning
Caution




Conformal
Preserves local angles and shapes at very small scales
Does not preserve area; Lambert Conformal Conic is an example


Equal-area
Preserves area relationships
Useful when area comparison matters; shapes can be distorted


Equidistant
Preserves specified distances, such as from a chosen center
Does not preserve every distance everywhere


Direction
Some projections preserve bearings from a chosen center
No flat map preserves every direction, area, and distance globally



Mercator is conformal and shows constant-bearing routes, or rhumb lines, as straight lines. That does not mean every straight line is the shortest route, or that all distances and directions between arbitrary points are preserved.


CRS codes used in class









EPSG
CRS
Units
Useful context




2272
NAD83 / Pennsylvania South (ftUS)
US survey feet
Local analysis around Philadelphia


5070
NAD83 / Conus Albers
Meters
Equal-area work across the contiguous United States


4326
WGS 84
Degrees
Common geographic coordinates


4269
NAD83
Degrees
Common in US geographic datasets


26918
NAD83 / UTM zone 18N
Meters
A projected option for Philadelphia



EPSG 2272 is specifically the US survey-foot version. It is not “feet or meters” interchangeably. A meter-based State Plane definition uses a different CRS code.
UTM divides the world into 60 numbered longitudinal zones, with northern and southern hemisphere versions. Zone numbers run from 1 to 60; there are no negative zone numbers. The hemisphere and datum matter as well as the zone. Large easting and northing values are normal and do not mean the coordinates are wrong.


Inspect, transform, or label?







Function
What it does




st_crs(x)
Reads the object’s CRS metadata


st_transform(x, 2272)
Converts coordinates from their known source CRS to the target CRS


st_set_crs(x, 4326)
Assigns or replaces a CRS label without moving the coordinates



The normal workflow is check the CRS, then transform if needed. There is no extra st_set_crs() step after st_transform().
The recording’s jar analogy helps: putting a “salt” label on a jar of sugar does not change what is inside. Likewise, calling st_set_crs(x, 2272) on longitude/latitude numbers does not convert them into feet. It only gives those same numbers a different interpretation. st_transform() performs the coordinate conversion and updates the label together.
Only use st_set_crs() when reliable information establishes what the existing coordinates already mean. Assigning a label to unknown coordinates by guesswork can place the data in the wrong location. sf transformation reference

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Bring in Indego Stations
Indego provides station locations through a live GeoJSON feed. This snapshot records when it was retrieved. It does not represent a historical 2023 station network merely because the income estimates end in 2023.

station_file <- file.path(data_dir, "indego-station-snapshot.rds")

if (file.exists(station_file)) {
  station_snapshot <- readRDS(station_file)
} else {
  station_snapshot <- list(
    retrieved_at = Sys.time(),
    data = st_read(
      "https://www.rideindego.com/stations/json/",
      quiet = TRUE
    )
  )
  saveRDS(station_snapshot, station_file)
}

stations <- station_snapshot$data %>%
  mutate(station_row = row_number())

[1] "US survey foot"

stopifnot(st_crs(philly_tracts) == st_crs(stations))

Here the reported units should be US survey feet. The lab uses 5,280 feet per mile, so its half-mile buffer is 2,640 coordinate feet. The distinction between a US survey foot and an international foot is tiny for this classroom buffer, but the CRS definition should still be recorded accurately.

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = philly_tracts, fill = "grey95", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, color = "#C43C39", size = 0.8) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Indego stations and Philadelphia tracts",
    subtitle = paste("Station snapshot:", as.Date(station_snapshot$retrieved_at))
  )








Later layers are drawn over earlier layers. Drawing the stations last makes them visible above the tract polygons. Some stations may lie outside the retained tracts; the next sections check this rather than assuming every station matches.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Spatial Operations: Match by Location
Table joins ask whether keys match. Spatial operations ask whether geometries have a relationship, such as intersecting, touching, containing, or being within a specified distance.

Predicates answer a relationship question







Function
Relationship tested




st_intersects(x, y)
The features share any point, including a boundary point


st_touches(x, y)
The boundaries meet, but the interiors do not intersect


st_within(x, y)
Each feature in x lies within a feature in y, according to the predicate’s boundary rules


st_contains(x, y)
The corresponding containment question with the roles reversed


st_disjoint(x, y)
The features share no points


st_is_within_distance(x, y, dist = ...)
Their minimum distance is within the supplied distance



st_touches() is more specific than everyday “touches.” A tract overlapping the inside of a station buffer intersects it; it usually does not satisfy st_touches(). Use st_intersects() when “any overlap or contact” is the intended rule. sf spatial predicates
For the classroom polygon example, imagine polygon B beside A with a shared edge, C entirely inside A, and D separated from A:



Relationship to A
Intersects A?
Touches A?
Within A?




B shares an edge, with no interior overlap
TRUE
TRUE
FALSE


C is entirely inside A, away from its boundary
TRUE
FALSE
TRUE


D is separated from A
FALSE
FALSE
FALSE



“Intersects” is the broad test. It includes containment as well as boundary contact and partial overlap. “Touches” excludes interior overlap.
The default result of many predicates is a sparse list of matching row positions. For example, the first element of st_intersects(tracts, stations) tells us which station rows intersect the first tract. lengths() counts matches for every element of that list. The singular length() would count the list’s elements, usually the number of input tracts.


Filter, join, or change the shapes?








Operation
Result
Does it cut the original shapes?




st_filter(x, y)
Selected whole features from x
No


st_join(x, y)
Features of x with matched attributes from y
No; rows may repeat for multiple matches


st_intersection(x, y)
Shared geometric portions
Yes


st_difference(x, y)
Portions of x outside y
Yes


st_sym_difference(x, y)
Portions belonging to one side but not both
Yes


st_union(x)
Combined geometry with internal overlap dissolved
Merges shapes


st_distance(x, y)
Distances between features
Returns measurements, not a new polygon layer



st_union() combines geometric coverage; it does not automatically add population or compute an income statistic. Likewise, st_intersection() can copy attributes to fragments, but it does not automatically estimate how many residents live in each fragment. sf geometry operations
Names can differ in meaning across GIS software. In this lab, the one-input st_union(x) dissolves the geometries together. Do not assume it produces the same attribute-preserving polygon subdivision as a desktop GIS tool named “Union.”


A spatial version of the overlapping-circle picture
Unlike the table-join diagram, this picture shows actual areas being combined or cut. The circles below are synthetic teaching shapes, not Indego results.

circle_a <- st_sfc(st_point(c(2600000, 240000)), crs = 2272) %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 800)
circle_b <- st_sfc(st_point(c(2601000, 240000)), crs = 2272) %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 800)

original_circles <- st_sf(geometry = c(circle_a, circle_b))

operation_shapes <- st_sf(
  operation = factor(
    c("Intersection: shared area", "Union: either circle",
      "Difference: A outside B", "Symmetric difference: one only"),
    levels = c("Intersection: shared area", "Union: either circle",
               "Difference: A outside B", "Symmetric difference: one only")
  ),
  geometry = c(
    st_intersection(circle_a, circle_b),
    st_union(c(circle_a, circle_b)),
    st_difference(circle_a, circle_b),
    st_sym_difference(circle_a, circle_b)
  )
)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = operation_shapes, fill = "#2A9D8F", color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = original_circles, fill = NA, color = "grey35") +
  facet_wrap(~operation, ncol = 2) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  theme_void()




Colored regions are the output of each operation. The gray outlines show the two original circles.

section: Spatial Join: Give Each Station Its Tract’s Attributes
text:
Spatial Join: Give Each Station Its Tract’s Attributes

stations_with_tract <- st_join(
  stations,
  philly_tracts %>% select(GEOID, med_incE, reliability),
  join = st_intersects,
  left = TRUE
)

This keeps station points and attaches the attributes of intersecting tracts. A station does not need its own GEOID beforehand. left = TRUE retains unmatched stations, which get missing tract attributes. A station on a shared boundary can intersect more than one tract and appear in more than one output row. sf spatial joins

Count stations per tract in two ways

station_counts <- stations_with_tract %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(GEOID)) %>%
  count(GEOID, name = "n_stations_from_join")

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(n_stations = lengths(st_intersects(., stations)))

  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, n_stations) %>%
  left_join(station_counts, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(n_stations_from_join = replace_na(n_stations_from_join, 0L))

Why the total can differ from the station count

station_matches <- st_intersects(stations, philly_tracts)

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
Distance to the Nearest Station

A tract needs a representative point

centroids <- st_centroid(st_geometry(philly_tracts))

We use each tract’s geometric centroid as a simple starting location. A centroid is not necessarily where most residents live, and it can fall outside an irregular polygon. st_point_on_surface() gives a point inside the polygon, but that point is not automatically a population center either.


All pairs versus one pair per tract

distance_matrix <- st_distance(centroids, stations)
dim(distance_matrix)

[1] 391 321

distance_matrix[
  seq_len(min(3, nrow(distance_matrix))),
  seq_len(min(3, ncol(distance_matrix))),
  drop = FALSE
]

Units: [US_survey_foot]
         [,1]     [,2]     [,3]
[1,] 4533.641 4669.516 12892.29
[2,] 5180.532 5051.223 13057.11
[3,] 9107.896 8324.892 14469.92


The rows represent tract centroids and the columns represent stations. Each cell is the distance for that pair. These measurements carry units. Without by_element = TRUE, this is a full matrix, not one distance per tract. Large all-pairs matrices can be expensive, so the next approach is more useful when we only need the nearest station. sf distance measurements
The geometries I pass in change the question. st_distance(philly_tracts, stations) measures the minimum distance between each polygon and each station, so a station inside a tract has distance zero from that tract. Using centroids instead measures from its representative point. Distance to a tract’s boundary or footprint and distance from its centroid are not interchangeable.

nearest_idx <- st_nearest_feature(centroids, stations)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    nearest_station = stations$name[nearest_idx],
    dist_ft = as.numeric(
      st_distance(
        centroids,
        stations[nearest_idx, ],
        by_element = TRUE
      )
    ),
    dist_mi = dist_ft / 5280
  )

summary(philly_tracts$dist_mi)

    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
 0.01893  0.15477  0.35357  1.74711  2.25126 10.93093 


nearest_idx contains station row positions, not distances. stations[nearest_idx, ] selects one matching station per tract, in tract order. by_element = TRUE then compares the first centroid with the first selected station, the second with the second, and so on.
If I were sorting distances manually, the nearest would be the smallest distance: ascending order. arrange(desc(distance)) would put the farthest first. st_nearest_feature() avoids building and sorting a full distance table for this task.
as.numeric() removes the units label after we have checked that the CRS uses feet. Dividing by 5,280 expresses the distance in the lab’s miles. These are straight-line distances, not walking routes. Rivers, rail yards, highways, entrances, and bridges can make a short straight-line distance a much longer journey.

ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = dist_mi), color = NA) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, inherit.aes = FALSE, size = 0.5, color = "white") +
  scale_fill_viridis_c() +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Distance from tract centroid to nearest Indego station",
    subtitle = "Straight-line distance; white points are stations",
    fill = "Miles"
  )

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Half-Mile Buffers: Filter Whole Tracts or Cut Their Shapes
text:
Half-Mile Buffers: Filter Whole Tracts or Cut Their Shapes
A buffer creates an area within a specified distance of a feature. Here each station gets a 2,640-foot circle. Unioning the buffers combines overlapping circles so shared areas are not counted repeatedly.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 2640) %>%
  st_union()

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = philly_tracts, fill = "grey95", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = station_zone, fill = "#56B4E9", color = NA, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, size = 0.4) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Half-mile zones around Indego stations",
    subtitle = "Overlapping station buffers have been dissolved into one geometry"
  )








The union can contain separated pieces in a MULTIPOLYGON. “One geometry” does not mean every station circle connects to every other one. sf buffers and other unary operations

st_filter(): keep the whole tract

tracts_near_stations <- st_filter(philly_tracts, station_zone)

outside_zone <- st_filter(
  philly_tracts,
  station_zone,
  .predicate = st_disjoint
)

tibble(
  relationship = c("Any intersection with zone", "No intersection with zone"),
  n_tracts = c(nrow(tracts_near_stations), nrow(outside_zone))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 2
  relationship               n_tracts
  <chr>                         <int>
1 Any intersection with zone      238
2 No intersection with zone       153


The default filter predicate is st_intersects(). A tract with even a tiny overlap, or just a shared boundary point, is selected whole. Its geometry is not trimmed to the buffer.
If the question instead asks for tracts entirely within the zone, make that predicate explicit:

entirely_within_zone <- st_filter(
  philly_tracts,
  station_zone,
  .predicate = st_within
)
nrow(entirely_within_zone)

[1] 171


st_filter() returns selected features. nrow() counts them. The function does not return a count by itself, and it does not require full containment unless we choose that relationship.
We use the unioned station zone for the disjoint test. Filtering for disjointness against individual station buffers could retain a tract simply because it is far from one station, even if it is beside another.


st_intersection(): keep only the covered portion

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  select(GEOID) %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  group_by(GEOID) %>%
  summarize(covered_area = sum(covered_area), .groups = "drop")

Warning: attribute variables are assumed to be spatially constant throughout
all geometries

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    covered_area = replace_na(covered_area, 0),
    pct_covered = if_else(
      tract_area > 0,
      100 * covered_area / tract_area,
      NA_real_
    )
  )

stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(philly_tracts$GEOID))
summary(philly_tracts$pct_covered)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
   0.00    0.00   88.81   53.98  100.00  100.00 


The steps are:

Measure each original tract’s area.
Cut the tract at the station-zone boundary.
Measure the retained portion and sum any fragments for that GEOID.
Drop geometry from the coverage table.
Join the measurements back to the original whole tracts.
Divide covered area by original area and multiply by 100.

Both areas use the same squared units, so the units cancel in the percentage. A tract with no intersecting portion has zero covered area. We join only one coverage record per GEOID to prevent duplicated tract rows.
We select only GEOID before the intersection because we need a spatial measurement, not copied income estimates on each fragment. An income estimate does not become an estimate for the clipped fragment just because its polygon was cut.
Some sf versions print a warning that attributes are assumed to be spatially constant when performing an overlay. Here the retained attribute is just the tract identifier. We are measuring clipped geometry, not assuming that income or population is evenly distributed inside the tract.

ggplot(philly_tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = pct_covered), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    labels = function(x) paste0(round(x), "%"),
    na.value = "grey80"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Tract area within half a mile of an Indego station",
    subtitle = "Area coverage is not the percentage of residents served",
    fill = "Area covered"
  )








A tract could be half covered by area while most homes are in its uncovered half. Water, industrial land, parks, and uneven settlement matter. This is an area-based indicator, not a direct resident-access rate.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Worked Challenge: Which Low-Income Tracts Lack Access?
text:
Worked Challenge: Which Low-Income Tracts Lack Access?
For this example:

Low income: a tract’s 2019–2023 median household income is at or below the 25th percentile among populated Philadelphia tracts with a known positive estimate.
Access: the tract centroid is within half a mile of its nearest station.

This is a relative citywide income definition, not an official poverty threshold. Ties at the cutoff can put slightly more than 25% of eligible tracts in the group. Missing income stays unknown and is not treated as high income.

known_income <- philly_tracts$med_incE[
  !is.na(philly_tracts$med_incE) & philly_tracts$med_incE > 0
]
stopifnot(length(known_income) > 0)

income_cutoff <- unname(quantile(known_income, probs = 0.25))

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    low_income = case_when(
      is.na(med_incE) | med_incE <= 0 ~ NA,
      TRUE ~ med_incE <= income_cutoff
    ),
    access_centroid = dist_mi <= 0.5,
    access_any_overlap = lengths(st_intersects(., station_zone)) > 0,
    access_half_area = pct_covered >= 50
  )

scales::dollar(income_cutoff)

[1] "$42,469"

philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarize(
    total_tracts = n(),
    income_status_unknown = sum(is.na(low_income)),
    low_income_tracts = sum(low_income, na.rm = TRUE),
    low_income_without_centroid_access = sum(
      low_income & !access_centroid,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

  total_tracts income_status_unknown low_income_tracts
1          391                    10                96
  low_income_without_centroid_access
1                                 33


The cutoff is calculated from this dataset. It will print above rather than being guessed in the notes. na.rm = TRUE excludes unknown values from the count; the separate unknown count makes that exclusion visible.

Map and list the selected tracts

low_income_no_access <- philly_tracts %>%
  filter(low_income, !access_centroid)

ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = philly_tracts, fill = "grey92", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = low_income_no_access, fill = "#D55E00", color = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = stations, color = "#0072B2", size = 0.6) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    title = "Low-income tracts with centroids over half a mile from Indego",
    subtitle = paste(
      "Income at or below", scales::dollar(income_cutoff),
      "| Orange: selected tracts; blue: stations"
    ),
    caption = paste("Station snapshot:", as.Date(station_snapshot$retrieved_at))
  )







low_income_no_access %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(dist_mi)) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, med_incE, med_incM, med_inc_cv,
         reliability, nearest_station, dist_mi) %>%
  head(15)

An income estimate with a CV of 45% remains in the selected list if its point estimate meets our income rule, but its reliability label will be “Low.” We should report that uncertainty. Silently dropping all uncertain tracts could hide communities with weak statistical coverage.
High sampling reliability also does not guarantee that a tract is clearly below a chosen cutoff. An estimate very close to the cutoff can have an interval that crosses it. This classification is a screening tool, not a definitive finding about every household.


Show the farthest selected tracts

farthest_selected <- low_income_no_access %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(dist_mi)) %>%
  slice_head(n = 15)

ggplot(
  farthest_selected,
  aes(x = reorder(GEOID, dist_mi), y = dist_mi, color = reliability)
) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Farthest low-income tracts under the centroid definition",
    subtitle = "Up to 15 tracts; color describes income reliability",
    x = "Tract GEOID",
    y = "Miles to nearest station",
    color = "Income reliability"
  )








reorder(GEOID, dist_mi) orders the labels by distance. coord_flip() makes those labels easier to read. The color refers to uncertainty in the income estimate, not uncertainty in the measured distance. If no tracts meet the definition, the table and plot will be empty rather than inventing a result.


Compare all three access definitions

access_comparison <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(low_income) %>%
  summarize(
    `Centroid within 0.5 mile` = sum(!access_centroid),
    `Any overlap with station zone` = sum(!access_any_overlap),
    `At least 50% of tract area covered` = sum(!access_half_area)
  ) %>%
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "access_definition",
    values_to = "low_income_without_access"
  )

access_comparison

  access_definition                  low_income_without_access
  <chr>                                                  <int>
1 Centroid within 0.5 mile                                  33

ggplot(
  access_comparison,
  aes(x = access_definition, y = low_income_without_access)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(aes(label = low_income_without_access), hjust = -0.15) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "The access definition changes the count",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Low-income tracts without access"
  )








Each row uses the same low-income group and station snapshot. Only the access rule changes. The any-overlap rule can classify a tract as served when the station zone covers just a small corner. The 50%-area rule demands more coverage but still makes no claim about where residents live. The centroid rule is easy to explain but reduces an entire tract to one point.
A possible defense of the worked choice is: I used centroid distance as a first screening measure because it gives each tract a comparable distance to its nearest station. It does not describe every resident’s journey, so I also compared overlap and area coverage to see how much the result depends on that choice.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: Extra Check: Does the Representative Point Matter?
text:
Extra Check: Does the Representative Point Matter?

inside_points <- st_point_on_surface(st_geometry(philly_tracts))
inside_nearest <- st_nearest_feature(inside_points, stations)
