title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
section: What We Can and Cannot Conclude
text:
What We Can and Cannot Conclude

Income: a tract median describes households collectively. It does not establish that every resident is low-income.
Sampling uncertainty: CV and MOE help describe uncertainty in the ACS estimate. They do not account for every possible source of error.
Location: an intersecting station, a nearby centroid, and a large covered area measure different things.
Travel: straight-line proximity does not measure walking time, safe crossings, or cycling conditions.
Service: a station point does not guarantee available bikes, available docks, affordable membership, or reliable service. The feed’s totalDocks field, if present, could support a separate capacity question.
Time: the station snapshot is contemporary to its download; the ACS estimates describe 2019–2023. This is not a reconstruction of 2023 service unless we obtain historical station data.
Boundaries: joining records is not the same as making different geography vintages comparable.

These checks help distinguish a useful screening map from a stronger claim about who Indego actually serves.

title: Week 4: Joins, Spatial Data, and Access to Indego
text:
My Mental Model
I start with a question, then decide what one row and one place represent. I check identifiers before a table join and coordinate systems before a spatial operation. I use a predicate to test a relationship, a filter to keep whole features, an overlay to create new shapes, and a join to attach attributes.
The biggest lesson from the lab is that “access” needs a definition. A map can look precise while hiding choices about boundaries, distance, population, and uncertainty. I need to state those choices so another person can understand what the result actually measures.

My September 18 class-note recap
My notes from September 18, 2026, reduce the workflow to a few checks I want to remember:

Join by the same GEOID. A left_join() keeps the left table’s rows and attaches matching columns. If a key does not match, the new value is NA; check the key type, duplicates, and row count.
Remember that geometry sticks. Selecting columns from an sf object usually keeps its geometry. Use st_drop_geometry() when I only need an ordinary attribute table.
Read the CRS before measuring. Geographic coordinates use longitude and latitude in degrees. Projected coordinates use eastings and northings in a local unit such as feet or meters. For Philadelphia, EPSG 2272 is NAD83 / Pennsylvania South in US survey feet; 5,280 feet make a mile.
Do not confuse labeling with conversion. st_crs() checks the metadata, st_transform() converts coordinates, and st_set_crs() only assigns a label to coordinates whose CRS is already known.
Choose the spatial operation by the question. Predicates such as st_intersects() test a relationship; st_filter() keeps whole features; st_intersection() cuts to shared areas; st_union() dissolves overlaps; st_join() attaches attributes by location.
Check the shape of distance output. st_distance(x, y) normally returns distances for every pair as a matrix. Find the nearest feature first and use by_element = TRUE when I need one matched distance per tract.

Those reminders connect my class shorthand to the full examples above. For example, a half-mile buffer in EPSG 2272 uses 2,640 feet, and the chosen predicate determines whether a tract merely touches the zone, overlaps it, or lies within it.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
This week focused on a question: Where are rents higher than we would expect given household income? We used regression to describe the relationship between income and rent, then considered how to check whether a model predicts well beyond the data used to fit it.
The main topics were linear regression, inference versus prediction, least squares, residuals, measurement error, training and test data, cross-validation, overfitting, and multicollinearity.






NoteAbout these notes and examples



I used made-up data for the examples so I can run them without the lab files. The lecture transcript did not include the full lab code. The example numbers below are for practice, not results from the lab.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
This week focused on a question: Where are rents higher than we would expect given household income? We used regression to describe the relationship between income and rent, then considered how to check whether a model predicts well beyond the data used to fit it.
The main topics were linear regression, inference versus prediction, least squares, residuals, measurement error, training and test data, cross-validation, overfitting, and multicollinearity.






NoteAbout these notes and examples



I used made-up data for the examples so I can run them without the lab files. The lecture transcript did not include the full lab code. The example numbers below are for practice, not results from the lab.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Starting with the Question
Suppose we observe the following illustrative values:



Annual household income
Monthly rent




$30,000
$1,000


$100,000
$3,000


$250,000
$6,000



These numbers suggest a positive relationship: places with higher incomes may also have higher rents. A model estimates that relationship across many observations. It does not assume every place with the same income has exactly the same rent.
For a tract-level analysis:

Outcome, response, or Y: median monthly rent.
Predictor, explanatory variable, or X: median annual household income.
Observation: one census tract.

Income and rent must refer to compatible geographies and periods. Annual income and monthly rent have different time units; that is acceptable in regression, but the labels and coefficient interpretation must make those units clear.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: The General Model: Y = f(X) + Epsilon
text:
The General Model: Y = f(X) + Epsilon
\[
Y = f(X) + \varepsilon
\]



Symbol
Meaning in the rent example




\(Y\)
The observed rent


\(X\)
The income information supplied to the model


\(f(X)\)
The systematic relationship between income and rent


\(\varepsilon\)
Variation not explained by that relationship



The symbol \(\varepsilon\) is called epsilon. A model using only income cannot account for everything affecting rent: housing quality, location, amenities, local supply, and other differences may matter.
If \(f(X)\) represents the true conditional mean, epsilon has mean zero conditional on X. Our fitted model may still miss systematic patterns because we chose an incomplete functional form or omitted useful predictors.
An error term and a residual are related but different: epsilon belongs to the underlying statistical model; a residual is a difference we calculate after fitting a model to observations.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Linear Regression
A simple linear regression takes the form:
\[
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_i + \varepsilon_i
\]

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept: the model’s expected Y when X equals zero.
\(\beta_1\) is the slope: the expected difference in Y associated with a one-unit increase in X.
\(i\) identifies an observation.

The fitted prediction is:
\[
\hat{Y}_i = \hat{\beta}_0 + \hat{\beta}_1 X_i
\]
A hat indicates an estimated quantity. We do not add an observed epsilon to make a prediction because that unexplained component is unknown.
For example, suppose an illustrative fitted model is:
\[
\widehat{\text{monthly rent}} = 500 + 0.02 \times \text{annual income}
\]
At an annual income of $50,000, predicted monthly rent is $1,500. The slope of 0.02 means an additional $1,000 in annual income is associated with $20 more in predicted monthly rent.
This is an association. It does not establish that raising a household’s income causes its rent to rise. A tract-level relationship also does not establish the same relationship for individual households.
The intercept may have little substantive meaning when zero income is far outside the observed data.

Checking Units in the Lecture Example
The transcript refers to an illustrative intercept of about 690 and a slope of 0.0081. If income is recorded in dollars, that would give:
\[
\widehat{\text{monthly rent}} = 690 + 0.0081 \times \text{annual income}
\]
An additional $10,000 of annual income would correspond to $81 more in predicted monthly rent: \(0.0081 \times 10{,}000 = 81\).
If we instead create an income column measured in units of $10,000, the equivalent slope becomes 81. The relationship and fitted predictions are unchanged; only the coefficient’s units change. These lecture numbers are illustrations, not the output of the practice model below.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Inference and Prediction








Goal
Question
Main focus




Inference
How is income associated with rent?
Coefficients, uncertainty, assumptions


Prediction
What rent should the model predict for another tract?
Accuracy on observations not used to fit the model



The note “B1 is inference” is shorthand. Beta 1 is a coefficient; inference is the process of learning about relationships and their uncertainty. Prediction uses estimated relationships to calculate outcomes.
A model can have a statistically significant slope and still make poor predictions. Likewise, a model may predict reasonably well while its individual coefficients are difficult to interpret.

The Main Emphasis of This Class
The professor contrasted this course’s emphasis on prediction with the emphasis on inference in our statistics course. We begin with linear regression because its mechanics are relatively easy to inspect. The same process of training, validation, and comparing errors can later be applied to other models.
A predictor does not have to pass an individual coefficient significance test to be useful for prediction. The question is whether it improves performance on appropriately held-out observations. However, trying many variables and repeatedly selecting the best validation result can itself overfit the validation data.


Variables, Features, and Targets
In this context, a feature is an input used for prediction. It may be an original column, such as income, or something derived from other data, such as distance to a university. The target is the outcome to predict, here rent. Not every column should be treated as a predictor: a tract identifier is usually for joining and labeling, for example.
Predicting a continuous amount such as monthly rent is a regression problem. Predicting a category such as whether a property is vacant is a classification problem. Logistic regression can serve the latter purpose despite having “regression” in its name.


The Bike-Share Example: Useful Prediction Is Not Causation
The professor used bike-share stations as an example of a possible predictor of rent. Their presence might reflect accessibility, destinations, investment, or other neighborhood characteristics. A station variable could act as a proxy, capturing information about those characteristics indirectly.
Even if adding station information improves predictions, we cannot conclude that installing a station would cause rents to increase. Stations may have been placed where those conditions already existed. Statistical significance would not resolve that causal question either.
Endogeneity refers to a predictor being correlated with the model’s error term, potentially because of omitted influences, reverse causation, or other mechanisms. It is different from multicollinearity, which concerns relationships among predictors. A useful prediction model alone is not sufficient evidence for a policy intervention.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Model Flexibility
More flexible models can represent more complicated relationships, but they can also follow accidental patterns in a particular sample.







Model family
Useful context




Linear regression
A relatively simple relationship, with directly interpretable coefficients


Ridge and lasso
Penalized regression that shrinks coefficients; lasso can set some to zero


Logistic regression
Usually used to model probabilities for a categorical outcome, such as yes/no


Decision trees
Divide the predictor space into regions using rules


Random forests
Combine many randomized trees


Boosting
Builds models sequentially to improve an overall prediction


Neural networks
Can learn complex relationships, depending on their architecture and training



This is not a fixed ranking from worst to best or rigid to flexible. Tree depth, penalties, network size, and other settings affect flexibility. Logistic regression is not simply the next step after linear regression for predicting continuous rent.
Parametric models specify a functional form with a fixed set of parameters, such as an intercept and slope. Nonparametric models do not restrict the relationship to that fixed form. Nonparametric does not mean “no assumptions” or “no quantities to estimate.”

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: How Least Squares Chooses the Line
text:
How Least Squares Chooses the Line
For each observation:
\[
e_i = y_i - \hat{y}_i
\]
Ordinary least squares chooses coefficients that minimize:
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
\]
These are vertical differences in the outcome, not the shortest perpendicular distances to the line. Squaring prevents positive and negative residuals from canceling and gives large errors more influence.
If two residuals are +$200 and -$200, their sum is zero, but their squared errors sum to 80,000 dollars squared. The fit should not treat those two errors as no error.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: A Practice Dataset That Runs on Its Own
text:
A Practice Dataset That Runs on Its Own
The following code creates 100 fictional tracts. The random variation represents differences the simple income model cannot explain.

set.seed(5080)

practice_tracts <- data.frame(
  tract_id = sprintf("Practice %03d", 1:100),
  med_inc = seq(30000, 150000, length.out = 100)
)

practice_tracts$med_rent <-
  600 + 0.015 * practice_tracts$med_inc + rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 180)

Fitting the Model in R

m1 <- lm(med_rent ~ med_inc, data = practice_tracts)

R is case-sensitive: use summary(m1), not Summary(m1). The lm() and summary() functions are available with a standard R installation.
The corresponding class example would be:
m1 <- lm(med_rent ~ med_inc, data = tracts)
summary(m1)
That last block is displayed for reference rather than executed because the real tracts object is not supplied in these notes.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Seeing the Fitted Line

plot(
  practice_tracts$med_inc,
  practice_tracts$med_rent,
  pch = 19,
  col = "steelblue",
  xlab = "Median annual household income ($)",
  ylab = "Median monthly rent ($)",
  main = "A linear model of rent and income"
)
abline(m1, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)







Figure 1: Invented practice data: monthly rent and annual household income.





Each point represents a fictional tract. The line gives the fitted rent at each income. Points above the line have positive residuals; points below it have negative residuals.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Reading summary(m1)







Output
How to read it




Estimate
The fitted coefficient


Std. Error
Estimated uncertainty in that coefficient


t value and Pr(>|t|)
A test of whether a coefficient is zero, under the model assumptions


Residual standard error
Residual variation, expressed in the outcome’s units


Multiple R-squared
The proportion of outcome variation explained in the fitting sample


Adjusted R-squared
An R-squared measure adjusted for the number of predictors



A small p-value does not tell me the relationship is causal or that the model will predict well elsewhere. Standard errors and tests depend on assumptions about the errors, including their dependence and variance.
For a test of a zero coefficient, the t statistic is the estimated coefficient divided by its standard error. The p-value concerns results at least as extreme under that null hypothesis and the test assumptions. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true. A zero slope means no linear association in the specified model; a nonlinear relationship could still exist.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Where Do Rents Exceed Expectations?
We calculate fitted rents and subtract them from observed rents:

practice_tracts$predicted_rent <- predict(m1, newdata = practice_tracts)
practice_tracts$residual <-
  practice_tracts$med_rent - practice_tracts$predicted_rent

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: Residuals Are Useful for Checking the Model
text:
Residuals Are Useful for Checking the Model

plot(
  fitted(m1), residuals(m1),
  pch = 19, col = "steelblue",
  xlab = "Fitted monthly rent ($)",
  ylab = "Observed minus fitted rent ($)",
  main = "Checking the residual pattern"
)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)







Figure 2: Practice residuals versus fitted rents.





A curved pattern can suggest missing nonlinearity. A widening spread can suggest changing error variance. An unusually large residual deserves investigation, but is not a reason to automatically delete an observation.
These checks complement predictive evaluation. A good-looking residual plot by itself is not proof of good performance on unseen data.

Homoskedasticity and Heteroskedasticity
Homoskedasticity means the conditional error variance is constant. Heteroskedasticity means it varies. For example, rent prediction errors might be much more spread out in high-income tracts than in middle-income tracts.
The professor emphasized that this pattern is useful information: our predictions may be less precise for some kinds of places. It is a reason to investigate those errors, consider useful predictors or a different functional form, and evaluate performance across groups.
A widening spread does not, by itself, prove an omitted variable or a biased conditional mean. Some outcomes are simply more variable in certain groups. Constant variance also does not mean residuals are independent, normally distributed, or free of systematic mean patterns; those are separate considerations.
For inference, heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors can change uncertainty estimates without changing the ordinary least-squares fitted line. They do not automatically improve its predictions. For prediction, adding features may help if there is learnable structure, but cannot guarantee constant error variance.


Outliers, Leverage, and Influence
A large residual means an observation’s outcome differs substantially from its prediction. High leverage means an observation has an unusual predictor value or combination of values. An influential observation materially changes the fitted model when removed. These are related ideas, but not synonyms. Investigate unusual points before deciding how to handle them.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: Measurement Error: Noise in Y and Noise in X
text:
Measurement Error: Noise in Y and Noise in X
ACS income and rent are estimates, so both can contain sampling error.
Noise in Y: independent, mean-zero measurement error in rent generally increases residual variation and reduces precision without systematically biasing the slope under the standard simple linear model assumptions.
Noise in X: in simple regression with classical additive, independent measurement error in income, the estimated slope is biased toward zero. This is called attenuation bias. A positive slope becomes flatter on average.
The qualification matters. Systematic or correlated errors, and models with several noisy predictors, can behave differently. It is not a universal rule that every kind of noise in X flattens every coefficient.
Ordinary lm() does not automatically incorporate ACS margins of error or correct predictor measurement error. Residuals can combine survey uncertainty with real differences and model misspecification.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Fit Versus Prediction
A model’s fit describes how well it represents the observations used to estimate it. Prediction asks how well it performs on observations it has not already seen.
The R-squared printed by summary(m1) describes in-sample fit. An R-squared of 0.80 means the fitted model explains 80% of the observed variation in Y around its mean in that sample. It does not mean 80% of predictions are correct.
For ordinary least squares with an intercept, adding predictors cannot lower training R-squared when the fitting observations remain the same. That makes training R-squared an insufficient basis for choosing a model.
An out-of-sample R-squared can also be calculated, but it is not the value automatically printed in the ordinary model summary. Unlike conventional training R-squared, out-of-sample R-squared can be negative.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Training and Test Data
Think of training data as practice questions and test data as new exam questions. Checking performance only on the practice questions can reward memorization.
We first reserve 20% of the fictional tracts as a test set. These rows should not guide model selection.

set.seed(25)

train_rows <- sample(
  seq_len(nrow(practice_tracts)),
  size = floor(0.8 * nrow(practice_tracts))
)

train_data <- practice_tracts[train_rows, c("tract_id", "med_inc", "med_rent")]
test_data <- practice_tracts[-train_rows, c("tract_id", "med_inc", "med_rent")]

c(training_rows = nrow(train_data), test_rows = nrow(test_data))

training_rows     test_rows 
           80            20 


The earlier full-data model was a demonstration of fitting and residuals. We do not reuse its fitted coefficients or predictions to evaluate this split. The following evaluation fits fresh models using training rows only.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Cross-Validation
Here CV means cross-validation. In our earlier ACS work, CV meant coefficient of variation. Context determines which meaning applies.
In K-fold cross-validation:

Divide the training observations into K groups called folds.
Hold out one fold for validation.
Fit a model on the other K minus one folds.
Predict the held-out observations and record their errors.
Repeat until each fold has been held out once.
Summarize the validation errors.

For 100 observations and five equal folds, each round fits on 80 observations and validates on 20. Every observation is used for validation once. For ten equal folds, each round fits on 90% and validates on 10% of the data assigned to cross-validation.
The separate test set stays outside this process. If I repeatedly inspect test results to choose a model, that set has become part of model selection.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Error Metrics: MAE and RMSE
\[
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i - \hat y_i|
\]
\[
\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat y_i)^2}
\]
Both metrics are in the outcome’s units, here dollars of monthly rent. Lower values mean smaller errors on the same evaluation data and outcome scale. RMSE gives greater influence to large errors. Neither guarantees that every prediction lies within that many dollars of the truth.
The lecture used being “off by about $300” to make RMSE understandable to a nontechnical audience. More precisely, an RMSE of $300 is a root-mean-squared error of $300; the mean absolute error need not be $300.
For errors of $100 and $300, MAE is $200, while RMSE is about $223.61. The larger error gets more weight in RMSE.
A loss function scores prediction errors. Ordinary least squares minimizes squared errors on the fitting data. A validation metric scores performance on held-out data. They can use related formulas, but the observations being scored are different.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
A Ten-Fold Practice Example
This example performs ten-fold validation within the 80-row training set. Each fold contains eight rows; each fitted model uses the other 72.

set.seed(5080)

fold_id <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(train_data)))
cv_predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(train_data))
fold_rmse <- numeric(10)

for (k in 1:10) {
  fitting_rows <- train_data[fold_id != k, ]
  validation_rows <- train_data[fold_id == k, ]

  fold_model <- lm(med_rent ~ med_inc, data = fitting_rows)

  cv_predictions[fold_id == k] <- predict(
    fold_model,
    newdata = validation_rows
  )

  fold_errors <- validation_rows$med_rent - cv_predictions[fold_id == k]
  fold_rmse[k] <- sqrt(mean(fold_errors^2))
}

cv_errors <- train_data$med_rent - cv_predictions

data.frame(
  metric = c("Pooled validation MAE", "Pooled validation RMSE",
             "Mean fold RMSE"),
  dollars = c(mean(abs(cv_errors)), sqrt(mean(cv_errors^2)),
              mean(fold_rmse))
)

                  metric  dollars
1  Pooled validation MAE 119.1101
2 Pooled validation RMSE 151.8495
3         Mean fold RMSE 149.9813

data.frame(fold = 1:10, RMSE = fold_rmse)

   fold     RMSE
1     1 123.8326
2     2 157.5209
3     3 144.4635
4     4 152.7003
5     5 192.7368
6     6 169.6636
7     7 126.4296
8     8 177.2673
9     9 114.4845
10   10 140.7135


How to read the loop:

k identifies the fold currently being held out.
!= k selects all the other folds for fitting.
== k selects the validation fold.
cv_predictions[fold_id == k] stores predictions in the positions belonging to that fold.

Each prediction comes from a model that did not fit on that observation. We combine all held-out errors to calculate the displayed metrics.
The transcript describes averaging the fold RMSEs. The code now reports that value as well as pooled RMSE, calculated from all held-out squared errors together. These are not generally equal because taking a square root and averaging are different operations. Use the same definition when comparing models, and inspect the fold results to see whether performance varies substantially between splits.
If comparing several models, use the same folds for each. Preprocessing that learns from data, such as imputation or scaling, must also be fitted inside each training fold. Otherwise validation information can leak into training.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Final Test-Set Evaluation
After selecting a model specification using training data, fit that specification to the full training set and evaluate once on the reserved test set. Here we demonstrate one linear specification, without a model-selection contest.

train_model <- lm(med_rent ~ med_inc, data = train_data)
test_predictions <- predict(train_model, newdata = test_data)
test_errors <- test_data$med_rent - test_predictions

# A simple benchmark: predict the training mean rent for every test tract.
baseline_predictions <- rep(mean(train_data$med_rent), nrow(test_data))
baseline_errors <- test_data$med_rent - baseline_predictions

data.frame(
  model = c("Income model", "Training-mean benchmark"),
  test_MAE = c(mean(abs(test_errors)), mean(abs(baseline_errors))),
  test_RMSE = c(
    sqrt(mean(test_errors^2)),
    sqrt(mean(baseline_errors^2))
  )
)

                    model test_MAE test_RMSE
1            Income model 121.9616  167.6737
2 Training-mean benchmark 476.1619  546.8125


The benchmark asks whether income improves prediction over simply using an average. Compare errors rather than assuming a fitted regression must be useful.

Which Regression Line Do We Keep After Cross-Validation?
This question came up in class. Each validation fold produces its own fitted line because it uses a different training subset. We normally do not choose the line from the fold with the smallest error. The folds help evaluate and choose a model specification, such as which predictors or penalty to use.
We then fit that chosen specification again using all the training data. If a separate test set was reserved, it remains untouched until final evaluation, as shown above.
After that evaluation, a model intended for use may be refitted on all available development observations, potentially including the former test set. If we do that, those rows no longer provide an independent test of the refitted model. We should retain and clearly report the earlier evaluation rather than present the new full-data fit as fresh evidence of predictive performance.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Overfitting and Underfitting
Overfitting occurs when a model learns sample-specific patterns, including noise, that do not generalize well. Training error can be very low while validation error is much larger.
Underfitting occurs when the model is too restrictive to capture useful structure. A straight line may miss a strongly curved relationship.
Increasing flexibility can reduce underfitting but increase sensitivity to the particular training sample. Validation helps choose an appropriate level of complexity. More complex does not automatically mean better, and a simple model can also perform poorly.
LOOCV, or leave-one-out cross-validation, is the case where K equals the number of observations. Each round holds out one observation. Ten-fold CV requires fewer fits and is often a practical alternative; LOOCV is not automatically superior.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
A Spatial Caution
Nearby tracts may share housing markets and other influences. Randomly splitting them can place very similar neighbors in training and validation sets, making evaluation optimistic for the task of predicting an entirely new area.
If the intended use is prediction in new regions, spatially separated folds may better represent that task. If predicting a future year, a time-based split may be more appropriate. The validation design should resemble the situation in which the model will be used.
The random splits above are appropriate for demonstrating the mechanics with independent invented observations; they do not establish that random CV is the best design for the real tract dataset.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Multicollinearity
The transcript gives important context to the rough note “mostly harmless.” The professor was discussing prediction, where a model may still be useful despite correlated predictors, provided validation supports it. That was not a claim that multicollinearity has no consequences.
Multicollinearity means one predictor can be closely approximated by a combination of other predictors. For example, median income and a strongly related income measure may contain overlapping information.
It can make individual coefficient estimates unstable and inflate their standard errors. With exact linear dependence, some coefficients cannot be uniquely estimated. It is therefore too broad to say it is “mostly harmless.”
For prediction within the same range and predictor relationships, the combined prediction can sometimes remain useful even when individual coefficients are unstable. Predictions may become unreliable when those relationships change or when extrapolating. Ridge regression is one possible response, chosen and evaluated according to the task.
In the one-predictor income model there are no multiple predictors to compete with one another. This issue becomes relevant as we add predictors.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
section: Connecting Back to the Rent Question
text:
Connecting Back to the Rent Question

Using Residuals to Create Better Features
The professor’s university example helps explain the original rent question: a neighborhood may have relatively low measured household income but high rents because students want to live near campus. Income alone may miss the influence of that location.
Feature engineering means constructing useful model inputs from available information. We might notice a pattern in training residuals and then test a feature that could capture it.








Pattern or idea
Possible feature
Question to test




Rent is underpredicted near universities
Distance to the nearest campus
Does adding distance reduce validation error?


Campus influence may be concentrated nearby
Indicator for being within a chosen campus buffer
Does this threshold work better than continuous distance?


Errors differ in very high-income areas
High-income indicator or nonlinear income term
Does it improve predictions for held-out observations?


Access or amenities may matter
Nearby station count or distance to a station
Does this information improve prediction beyond income?



The transcript mentions flagging the highest-income neighborhoods with a binary variable. Binary means 0 or 1: for example, 1 for an observation meeting a stated income rule and 0 otherwise. This is a hypothesis to test, not a guaranteed fix.
It is more useful to define a reproducible rule based on available predictors than to mark a handful of tract IDs just because the model missed them. An ID-specific fix can memorize the training sample and fail elsewhere.
If a threshold is estimated from the data, such as the top income percentile, estimate it from each training fold and apply that rule to its validation fold. Do not use validation rents to create predictor values. Features must also be available when making the intended future prediction.


Connecting Feature Engineering to Week 4
Our spatial tools can help construct these features:

st_distance() supplies distances that can be reduced to the nearest relevant feature.
st_buffer() creates a proximity zone, with a suitable CRS and distance units.
st_intersects() identifies which geometries meet that zone.
st_join() attaches attributes using a specified spatial relationship.

The precise definition matters. The distance from an entire tract polygon to a campus can be zero if they intersect. Distance from a tract centroid is a different measure. Similarly, “any part of the tract intersects a half-mile buffer” does not mean every resident lives within half a mile.
These are modeling choices that should be documented and evaluated, not interchangeable ways to describe proximity.


Comparing Candidate Features Fairly
Start with the income-only baseline. Evaluate a candidate model with the same folds and metric, compare its errors with the baseline, and inspect where it improves or worsens predictions. A tiny improvement on one split can be chance variation; there is no universal RMSE cutoff that defines a good model.
Use training and validation results to make these choices. Keep the final test set for the final assessment. A nonsignificant coefficient is not an automatic reason to remove a useful predictor, and a significant coefficient is not an automatic reason to keep a poor predictor.


Philadelphia Versus Miami
The class discussed whether a rent model built for Philadelphia would work in Miami. This is a question about generalization: will the learned relationship remain useful in the intended setting?
Miami may have different predictor distributions and rent relationships, including the relevance of beach proximity. Poor transfer can result from distribution shift, even if the model was not overfit within Philadelphia. Strong local validation does not guarantee accuracy in another city.
A model intended for one city can use locally meaningful features. A model intended for multiple cities needs consistently defined, available inputs and evaluation that represents those new cities. The desired use determines what kind of validation is convincing.


A Practical Workflow
To study rents above the model’s expectation, I would:

Define the geography, period, rent measure, and income measure.
Check missing values, ACS reliability, and whether variables describe compatible populations.
Plot income against rent and fit a baseline model.
Examine coefficients and residual patterns.
Evaluate prediction with a suitable validation design.
Calculate and map residuals, stating whether they are fitted or held-out prediction errors.
Investigate places with large positive residuals without treating those residuals as proof of a cause.

For the real lab, I should retain the professor’s supplied workflow and adapt the variable names and data preparation to that file. The practice examples here explain the mechanics but do not replace the lab dataset or instructions.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Cross-Validation
text:
Corrections to Remember







Rough note
More precise version




“B1 is inference”
Beta 1 is a slope parameter; inference concerns relationships and uncertainty.


“Noise in X flattens the slope”
This holds under classical measurement-error assumptions in simple regression.


“R-squared tells us prediction quality”
The usual model summary reports training fit; evaluate unseen-data predictions separately.


“Multicollinearity is mostly harmless”
It can undermine coefficient interpretation and sometimes prediction.


“CV” always means the same thing
Here it means cross-validation; previously it meant coefficient of variation.


“Positive residual means overpriced”
It means higher than this model predicts, which requires further interpretation.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
These notes follow the Philadelphia house-price example and its spatial diagnostics. The R chunks are study examples and are not executed when this page renders. The figures retain the example outputs; lecture-reported values are identified separately in the text.
This week moves from predicting median rent for census tracts to predicting prices for individual houses. The main question is whether the model makes similar mistakes in nearby places.
A model can have a reasonable overall error and still consistently undervalue houses in one area and overvalue houses in another. Residual maps show where those mistakes occur. Moran’s I measures whether nearby errors tend to resemble one another.
We also build two kinds of spatial features: counts within a buffer and distances to nearby events. The Philadelphia example leads into the Chicago house-price prediction assignment.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
These notes follow the Philadelphia house-price example and its spatial diagnostics. The R chunks are study examples and are not executed when this page renders. The figures retain the example outputs; lecture-reported values are identified separately in the text.
This week moves from predicting median rent for census tracts to predicting prices for individual houses. The main question is whether the model makes similar mistakes in nearby places.
A model can have a reasonable overall error and still consistently undervalue houses in one area and overvalue houses in another. Residual maps show where those mistakes occur. Moran’s I measures whether nearby errors tend to resemble one another.
We also build two kinds of spatial features: counts within a buffer and distances to nearby events. The Philadelphia example leads into the Chicago house-price prediction assignment.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Review: interpreting a logged predictor
Suppose the fitted relationship is:
\[
\widehat{rent} = \hat\beta_0 + 210\log(income).
\]
Rent remains in dollars, but income is logged. A 1% increase in income corresponds to approximately:
\[
210 / 100 = \$2.10
\]
more predicted monthly rent, holding any other predictors fixed. The exact change is 210 * log(1.01), about $2.09. A 10% increase corresponds to 210 * log(1.10), about $20.02, rather than exactly ten times the 1% approximation.
The log allows a curved relationship with income in its original dollar units. An additional $10,000 represents a much larger percentage increase from $20,000 than from $200,000. Whether this improves predictions is a question for cross-validation, not something the transformation guarantees.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Review: the factor level that broke a fold
text:
Review: the factor level that broke a fold
Error: factor district has new levels Upper Far Northeast
This means the validation data contain a category that the fitted model did not see in training. If all observations from a small district are held out together, the model has no estimated coefficient for that district.
Possible responses include a defensible merge of small groups, a coarser geography, or a model that can handle new groups. Simply listing a category as a factor level does not create information to estimate its coefficient.
There are many more neighborhoods than planning districts, so sparse categories become a bigger issue in house-level analysis. Count group sizes and check training coverage in every fold. If grouping rules are chosen using outcomes, they must be learned within training folds; preset geographic groupings should also make sense for the intended prediction task.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: From census tracts to individual houses
text:
From census tracts to individual houses








Question
Tract analysis
House analysis




What is one observation?
A tract
A property record with a sale price


What geometry represents it?
Polygon
Point


How might we count nearby incidents?
Within the tract boundary
Within a buffer around the house


How might we measure accessibility?
Distance to a station
Distance to the nearest station or average distance to several stations


What is the outcome?
Median rent
Sale price



A buffer is a polygon constructed around a feature at a specified distance. Around a point, a planar buffer approximates a circle. A 660-foot buffer has a radius of 660 feet, or one eighth of a mile. Its diameter is 1,320 feet.
A buffer is based on straight-line distance. It does not represent a walking route or account for barriers such as rivers and highways.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Packages and the data-query helper

library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(spdep)
library(nngeo)

options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0(
    "https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=",
    URLencode(sql, reserved = TRUE)
  )
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}








Package
Role




tidyverse
Clean tables, create features, and draw charts


sf
Read spatial data, transform coordinates, make buffers, and map geometry


nngeo
Find nearest features and their distances


spdep
Build spatial weights, calculate spatial lags, and assess spatial autocorrelation



options(scipen = 999) discourages scientific notation in printed numbers; it does not change their values.
carto_get() is a custom function. Its input is a SQL query stored as text. paste0() constructs the request URL, URLencode() makes the query suitable for a URL, and st_read() reads the returned GeoJSON into an sf object.
The function definition stores the instructions. The data request happens when we call carto_get(...).

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Download Philadelphia property records

sales_raw <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, parcel_number, sale_price, sale_date,
          total_livable_area, number_of_bedrooms,
          number_of_bathrooms, year_built, interior_condition
   FROM opa_properties_public
   WHERE category_code = '1'
     AND sale_date >= '2023-01-01'
     AND sale_date < '2025-01-01'"
) %>%
  st_transform(2272)

The SQL has three main parts:

SELECT names the columns to return. the_geom contains geometry.
FROM identifies the source table.
WHERE limits the records to the chosen property category and sale-date range.

The start date is included and the end date is excluded. This covers 2023 and 2024, not 2025.
This query uses the sale fields in the OPA property table. We should not assume it is a complete transaction history of every sale a parcel has ever had. It is also a live source, so later updates can change the returned records.

nrow(sales_raw)
summary(sales_raw$sale_price)
st_crs(sales_raw)$units_gdal

sales_raw %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(parcel_number, sale_price, sale_date, total_livable_area) %>%
  head()

The lecture output contained 37,866 records, with a minimum price of $0, median of $190,000, and maximum of $15,428,633. These describe the lecture’s downloaded data before cleaning; they are not model performance statistics.
st_transform(2272) puts the Philadelphia data in Pennsylvania South State Plane coordinates, measured in US survey feet. This matters because the buffer radius of 660 is interpreted in the projected coordinate units.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Not every recorded transfer is a market sale
text:
Not every recorded transfer is a market sale
Very low prices can reflect family transfers or other transactions that do not represent an ordinary market purchase. Other unusual sales may also require attention. A price cutoff is a practical screening rule, not proof that every retained record is an arm’s-length sale.

sales_raw %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(
    price_band = cut(
      sale_price,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 1000, 10000, 50000, Inf),
      labels = c("Up to $1,000", "Over $1,000–$10,000",
                 "Over $10,000–$50,000", "Over $50,000")
    )
  )

With the default cut() settings, an interval includes its upper boundary. A sale at exactly $1,000 belongs to the first band. This exploratory grouping is separate from the cleaning cutoff below, which retains prices at exactly $10,000.

Apply cleaning rules and show their effect

sales_market <- sales_raw %>%
  filter(is.finite(sale_price), sale_price >= 10000)

sales_space <- sales_market %>%
  filter(
    is.finite(total_livable_area),
    total_livable_area > 0,
    !st_is_empty(geometry),
    st_geometry_type(geometry) == "POINT"
  )

sales <- sales_space %>%
  mutate(
    year_built = na_if(as.numeric(year_built), 0),
    age = 2024 - year_built
  ) %>%
  filter(
    is.finite(age), age >= 0,
    is.finite(number_of_bathrooms), number_of_bathrooms >= 0
  ) %>%
  arrange(parcel_number, sale_date, sale_price) %>%
  mutate(record_id = row_number())

cleaning_log <- tibble(
  stage = c("Downloaded", "Price at least $10,000",
            "Positive area and point geometry", "Usable age and bathrooms"),
  remaining = c(nrow(sales_raw), nrow(sales_market),
                nrow(sales_space), nrow(sales))
) %>%
  mutate(removed_at_step = lag(remaining, default = first(remaining)) - remaining)

cleaning_log

na_if(year_built, 0) treats a recorded construction year of zero as unknown. age = 2024 - year_built is a common reference-year age, following the class example. It is not exactly age at sale for every observation.
The lecture retained 27,551 records. The checks here also require finite values, nonnegative ages and bathroom counts, and point geometry. The cleaning log reports the actual retained sample.
We do not remove every expensive house simply because it is hard to predict. Any upper-price cutoff needs a reason tied to the population we intend to model. Record the number of rows removed and consider whose homes are being excluded.


Check repeated properties and locations

sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(parcel_number) %>%
  filter(n > 1) %>%
  head(10)

coords <- st_coordinates(sales)

tibble(
  records = nrow(sales),
  repeated_coordinate_rows = sum(duplicated(coords))
)

Multiple rows at the same point might represent repeated property records, shared geocoding, or distinct units. They need inspection, not automatic deletion. Repeated records from the same property should not be split between training and validation if that would let the model recognize the same property on both sides.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Create spatial predictors from incident locations
text:
Create spatial predictors from incident locations

violent <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01'
     AND dispatch_date < '2025-01-01'
     AND text_general_code IN (
       'Aggravated Assault Firearm',
       'Aggravated Assault No Firearm',
       'Robbery Firearm',
       'Robbery No Firearm'
     )"
) %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(geometry), st_geometry_type(geometry) == "POINT") %>%
  st_transform(2272)

stopifnot(nrow(violent) >= 5)

IN (...) selects records whose category matches one of the listed values. The object name violent is shorthand for these selected assault and robbery categories, not a count of every possible violent offense.
Both layers must use the same CRS. We are relating house points to incident points using distance, not joining them by a shared ID.

Feature A: incidents inside a fixed buffer

sales <- sales %>%
  mutate(
    violent_660ft = lengths(
      st_intersects(st_buffer(geometry, dist = 660), violent)
    )
  )

summary(sales$violent_660ft)

There are three nested operations:

st_buffer() draws a 660-foot buffer around each house.
st_intersects() returns a list of incident-row indices that intersect each buffer.
lengths() counts the matches in each list element.

lengths() is plural because it measures each element of the list. length() would give one number: the length of the list itself.
If a house has no selected incidents within its buffer, its count is zero. An incident can be counted for several nearby houses because their buffers overlap. That is expected for a proximity feature; summing the house counts would not give a citywide count of unique incidents.


Feature B: average distance to the five nearest incidents

incident_neighbors <- st_nn(
  sales,
  violent,
  k = 5,
  returnDist = TRUE,
  progress = FALSE
)

stopifnot(all(lengths(incident_neighbors$dist) == 5))

sales$violent_knn5 <- vapply(incident_neighbors$dist, mean, numeric(1))

sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(record_id, violent_660ft, violent_knn5) %>%
  head()

k = 5 requests five neighbors per house. $dist selects the returned distance lists. vapply(..., mean, numeric(1)) calculates one numeric mean per house; it serves the same purpose as the lecture’s sapply(..., mean) with an explicit expected output type.
For projected point inputs, this nearest-neighbor calculation uses the coordinate scale. Here the distances are in US survey feet. Always check the CRS rather than assuming all spatial distances are meters.









Feature
What is fixed?
What varies?
Interpretation




violent_660ft
Radius: 660 feet
Number of incidents
More means more selected incidents nearby


violent_knn5
Number of incidents: five
Average distance
Smaller means selected incidents are closer



The kNN feature can distinguish houses whose buffer counts are both zero. It still finds the nearest incidents even if they are far away. Unlike a fixed buffer, its geographic reach expands in sparse areas.
A nearest-neighbor distance can be zero when features share coordinates; the average of five distances can also be zero if all five coincide with the house. “kNN is never zero” is a useful classroom contrast with zero counts, but not a mathematical guarantee.

sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(violent_660ft, violent_knn5) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ feature, scales = "free", ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Feature value: incident count or distance in feet", y = "Houses")


These are contextual predictors, not proof that crime causes the observed price differences. Reporting patterns, geocoding quality, omitted neighborhood characteristics, and the selected crime categories all affect their meaning.
Timing matters: the class example uses 2023–2024 incidents for 2023–2024 sales. For a genuinely forward-looking prediction at a sale date, some of those incidents would not yet be known. Historical predictors should use information available before the prediction date. A feature can leak future information even when it is not a price variable.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Fit the house-price model

model_data <- sales %>% st_drop_geometry()

f_knn <- sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age + violent_knn5

m1 <- lm(f_knn, data = model_data, na.action = na.fail)

sales$pred <- as.numeric(predict(m1, newdata = model_data))
sales$resid <- sales$sale_price - sales$pred

summary(m1)

The formula models sale price using floor area, bathrooms, age, and mean distance to nearby incidents. The outcome remains in dollars. An intercept is included by default.
na.action = na.fail stops if a required value is missing. This prevents the fitted model from silently using a different row set from the spatial weights or residual map.
These predictions come from a model fitted to the same observations. They are in-sample fitted values. They help diagnose the model, but do not replace held-out evaluation.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Understand the sign of a residual
text:
Understand the sign of a residual
\[
residual = actual - predicted.
\]



Actual price
Predicted price
Residual
Meaning




$300,000
$250,000
+$50,000
Model predicted too low


$300,000
$350,000
−$50,000
Model predicted too high


$300,000
$300,000
$0
Exact fitted value



Positive residual = underprediction. Negative residual = overprediction.
This sign convention matters for assessment fairness. A home the model overvalues has a negative actual-minus-predicted residual. Whether that translates into a higher tax bill depends on how the assessment and tax system uses the valuation.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Map where the model is wrong
text:
Map where the model is wrong

ggplot(sales) +
  geom_sf(aes(color = resid), size = 0.4, alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac",
    mid = "grey90",
    high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-300000, 300000),
    oob = scales::squish,
    labels = scales::label_dollar()
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(
    color = "Residual",
    title = "Where the model is wrong",
    subtitle = "Red: predicted too low. Blue: predicted too high.",
    caption = "In-sample residuals. Colors saturate outside ±$300,000."
  )


alpha controls transparency so overlapping points are easier to see. midpoint = 0 centers the diverging palette on a correct prediction.
scales::squish assigns values outside the color limits to the end colors. It does not change the residuals, remove expensive houses, or cap errors in RMSE. A −$900,000 residual and a −$300,000 residual receive the same end color, so inspect the numeric extremes too.

sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(resid))) %>%
  select(parcel_number, sale_price, pred, resid) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

Clusters of red suggest places the model tends to underpredict; clusters of blue suggest places it tends to overpredict. They may point to missing features or an unsuitable model form, but a map alone does not identify the cause.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Spatial autocorrelation
Spatial autocorrelation describes how a variable relates to itself across locations. Here the variable is the model residual.

Positive spatial autocorrelation: nearby errors tend to have similar values.
Negative spatial autocorrelation: nearby errors tend to differ.
Little global spatial autocorrelation: no strong overall association under the chosen neighborhood definition.

For example, if five nearby houses are all underpredicted by roughly $80,000, the model may be missing a local amenity, property characteristic, or relationship that differs in that area.
Global absence of a pattern is not proof that all errors are independent. Local clusters can cancel one another in an overall statistic, and patterns depend on the scale at which neighbors are defined.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Two different uses of kNN
kNN means k nearest neighbors. It is a way of selecting nearby observations, not automatically a particular prediction model.









Use
Starting point
Neighbors
Purpose




Spatial predictor
House
Five incident locations
Measure proximity to selected incidents


Residual diagnostic
House
Five other houses
Compare the house’s error with nearby errors



The first becomes a model input. The second helps evaluate model errors. Neighboring residuals require observed outcomes, so they are not an available predictor for a new house whose price is unknown.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Build a spatial weights object

coords <- st_coordinates(sales)
stopifnot(nrow(coords) == nrow(sales), nrow(coords) > 5, all(is.finite(coords)))

has_duplicate_locations <- anyDuplicated(coords) > 0

house_knn <- knearneigh(
  coords,
  k = 5,
  longlat = FALSE,
  use_kd_tree = !has_duplicate_locations
)

house_nb <- knn2nb(house_knn)
w_knn <- nb2listw(house_nb, style = "W")

table(card(house_nb))
head(vapply(w_knn$weights, sum, numeric(1)))

The steps are:

st_coordinates() extracts each house’s projected X and Y coordinates.
knearneigh(..., k = 5) identifies five other nearby houses, excluding the observation itself.
knn2nb() converts those indices to a neighbor-list object.
nb2listw(..., style = "W") assigns row-standardized weights.

With five equally weighted neighbors, each receives weight 1/5 = 0.2, and each row’s weights sum to one. card() reports each observation’s number of neighbors.
Duplicate coordinates can produce warnings and distance ties. The code turns off the kd-tree path when duplicates are present, but this does not resolve the substantive question of why multiple records share a location. Ties can make neighbor selection sensitive to record order.
A kNN relation is not necessarily mutual: B can be among A’s five closest houses without A being among B’s five closest. Symmetrizing the graph changes the neighbor definition and may give some houses more than five neighbors.
Do not sort or remove rows after building w_knn and then apply it to a differently ordered residual vector. The neighbor indices refer to the existing row positions. Rebuild weights if the analysis sample changes.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: The spatial lag: a weighted average of nearby values
text:
The spatial lag: a weighted average of nearby values

sales$resid_lag <- lag.listw(w_knn, sales$resid)

sales %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(record_id, resid, resid_lag) %>%
  head()

Here resid_lag is the average residual of each house’s five neighbors. “Lag” means a value calculated using spatial neighbors; it does not mean the previous row or the previous year.
If a house’s five neighbors have residuals of $10,000, $20,000, $30,000, $40,000, and $50,000, its spatial lag is $30,000. Its own residual is not included.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Compare my error with my neighbors’ errors
text:
Compare my error with my neighbors’ errors

ggplot(sales, aes(x = resid, y = resid_lag)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, color = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.15, size = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#b2182b") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-300000, 300000), ylim = c(-200000, 200000)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Do nearby houses have similar prediction errors?",
    x = "House residual: actual minus predicted",
    y = "Average residual of five neighboring houses"
  )









Part of the plot
Interpretation




Upper right
House and neighbors are underpredicted


Lower left
House and neighbors are overpredicted


Upper left
House is overpredicted while neighbors are underpredicted


Lower right
House is underpredicted while neighbors are overpredicted



The reference lines are at zero. For general variables, Moran scatterplots use deviations from the overall mean. An ordinary least-squares model with an intercept has in-sample residuals whose mean is approximately zero.
coord_cartesian() zooms the visible region while retaining the full dataset for the fitted line. It does not restrict the observations used for Moran’s I.
With row-standardized weights and a neighbor for every observation, the slope of the spatial-lag-versus-value regression corresponds to Moran’s I. The weighting convention matters.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Moran’s I, one part at a time
text:
Moran’s I, one part at a time
\[
I = \frac{n}{S_0}
\frac{\sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}(x_i-\bar{x})(x_j-\bar{x})}
{\sum_i(x_i-\bar{x})^2},
\qquad S_0 = \sum_i\sum_j w_{ij}.
\]



Symbol
Meaning in this analysis




n
Number of houses


x_i
Residual for house i


x̄
Mean residual


w_ij
Weight connecting house i to house j


S₀
Sum of all weights



The numerator multiplies deviations at neighboring locations. Two positive deviations make a positive product; two negative deviations also make a positive product. Opposite signs make a negative product. The denominator scales by the overall variation in the values.
The question is: when a house’s error is above average, are its neighbors’ errors also above average?
For row-standardized weights with no isolated observations, every row sums to one, so S₀ = n and the leading fraction equals one.

Five houses on a block
Use the lecture’s residuals, expressed in thousands of dollars:

block_example <- tibble(
  house = LETTERS[1:5],
  residual_thousands = c(100, 80, 20, -50, -70)
) %>%
  mutate(deviation = residual_thousands - mean(residual_thousands))

block_example

The mean is +16, so the deviations are +84, +64, +4, −66, and −86. Define neighbors as the houses immediately next door: A–B, B–C, C–D, and D–E.



Pair
Product of deviations




A–B
84 × 64 = 5,376


B–C
64 × 4 = 256


C–D
4 × −66 = −264


D–E
−66 × −86 = 5,676



The products sum to 11,044. With a binary, symmetric neighbor matrix, each pair is counted in both directions. The numerator is therefore 22,088 and the sum of weights is eight.
The sum of squared deviations is 22,920:
\[
I = \frac{5}{8}\frac{22088}{22920} \approx 0.6023.
\]

z_block <- block_example$deviation
W_binary <- matrix(0, nrow = 5, ncol = 5)

for (i in 1:4) {
  W_binary[i, i + 1] <- 1
  W_binary[i + 1, i] <- 1
}

I_binary <- (length(z_block) / sum(W_binary)) *
  as.numeric(t(z_block) %*% W_binary %*% z_block) / sum(z_block^2)

W_row <- W_binary / rowSums(W_binary)
I_row <- (length(z_block) / sum(W_row)) *
  as.numeric(t(z_block) %*% W_row %*% z_block) / sum(z_block^2)

tibble(
  weights = c("Binary next-door weights", "Row-standardized next-door weights"),
  morans_I = c(I_binary, I_row)
)

The row-standardized version is about 0.7229. The result differs because the end houses have one neighbor while interior houses have two. The hand calculation uses binary weights; the house-price analysis uses row-standardized kNN weights. We should not switch between these conventions without saying so.


Interpreting the statistic
Positive I indicates similar neighboring deviations overall. Negative I indicates a tendency toward contrasting neighboring deviations. Near-zero I suggests little overall spatial association at the chosen scale.
Moran’s I is not a percentage of variance explained. It does not mean “26% of houses are clustered” when I is 0.26. Its attainable range depends on the weights; it is not universally bounded exactly by −1 and +1 like an ordinary correlation coefficient.
Under a random-permutation null, its expected value is -1 / (n - 1), which is close to zero for a large dataset. A global value close to that expectation does not rule out local patterns.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Shuffle the residuals to assess the observed pattern
text:
Shuffle the residuals to assess the observed pattern

set.seed(5080)

mc <- moran.mc(
  sales$resid,
  w_knn,
  nsim = 499,
  alternative = "greater"
)

tibble(
  morans_I = unname(mc$statistic),
  permutation_p = mc$p.value,
  permutations = 499
)

The locations and neighbor connections stay fixed. The function shuffles the residual values among those locations 499 times and compares the observed I with the simulated values.
alternative = "greater" asks whether the observed association is unusually positive. It is not a two-sided test for every possible spatial pattern.
The lecture reported I = 0.2605251 and p = 0.002. That is evidence of positive residual clustering relative to this permutation reference. With 499 permutations, 1/500 = 0.002 is the smallest attainable conventional permutation p-value. It is not the probability that the model is correct or that the pattern happened “by luck.”

permutation_values <- tibble(I = head(mc$res, -1))

ggplot(permutation_values, aes(x = I)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "grey70", color = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = unname(mc$statistic), color = "firebrick", linewidth = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Observed clustering compared with shuffled residuals",
    subtitle = "Red line: observed Moran’s I",
    x = "Moran’s I",
    y = "Permutations"
  )


With many observations, even small patterns can produce small p-values. Track the magnitude of I alongside prediction error. Residual permutation is useful here as a diagnostic; formal regression inference also needs assumptions about residual exchangeability and the fitted model.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Cross-validation and the model log
The lecture fits the example model to map its errors. For comparing predictive features, we also need out-of-fold predictions. This extension evaluates a house-only baseline, buffer count, kNN distance, and both spatial predictors using the same observations and folds.
Repeated records with a known parcel number are kept together in a fold. This avoids putting the same known property in training and validation. Spatially separated folds would answer a different question about transfer to new areas.

model_data <- sales %>% st_drop_geometry()

property_group <- if_else(
  is.na(model_data$parcel_number) | as.character(model_data$parcel_number) == "",
  paste0("unknown-record-", model_data$record_id),
  paste0("parcel-", as.character(model_data$parcel_number))
)

unique_properties <- unique(property_group)
stopifnot(length(unique_properties) >= 10)

set.seed(5080)
property_folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = length(unique_properties)))
fold_id <- property_folds[match(property_group, unique_properties)]

table(fold_id)


cv_predictions <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  stopifnot(nrow(data) == length(fold_id), !anyNA(fold_id))
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))

  for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
    validation <- fold_id == k
    fit <- lm(formula, data = data[!validation, ], na.action = na.fail)
    predictions[validation] <- predict(fit, newdata = data[validation, ])
  }

  stopifnot(all(is.finite(predictions)))
  predictions
}

morans_i <- function(values, weights) {
  moran(
    values,
    weights,
    n = length(values),
    S0 = Szero(weights)
  )$I
}

Each house is predicted by a model that did not train on its fold. The predictions are returned in the original row order. This order must also match the spatial weights.

formulas <- list(
  House_only = sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age,
  Buffer_count = sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age + violent_660ft,
  KNN_distance = f_knn,
  Both_features = sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age +
    violent_660ft + violent_knn5
)

evaluations <- lapply(formulas, function(f) {
  fit <- lm(f, data = model_data, na.action = na.fail)
  oof_pred <- cv_predictions(f, model_data, fold_id)
  oof_resid <- model_data$sale_price - oof_pred

  list(
    oof_pred = oof_pred,
    oof_resid = oof_resid,
    cv_rmse = sqrt(mean(oof_resid^2)),
    moran_in_sample = morans_i(residuals(fit), w_knn),
    moran_out_of_fold = morans_i(oof_resid, w_knn)
  )
})

model_log <- imap_dfr(evaluations, function(result, model_name) {
  tibble(
    model = model_name,
    cv_rmse = result$cv_rmse,
    moran_in_sample = result$moran_in_sample,
    moran_out_of_fold = result$moran_out_of_fold
  )
})

model_log %>%
  arrange(cv_rmse) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = c(0, 2, 3, 3))

The log records which residuals were used for Moran’s I. In-sample and out-of-fold residual diagnostics are different quantities. Do not compare them as if they were interchangeable.



Metric
Question




CV RMSE
How large are held-out prediction errors, in dollars?


In-sample Moran’s I
Do errors from the fitted model cluster?


Out-of-fold Moran’s I
Do held-out prediction errors cluster?



Lower RMSE is better on that scoring rule. Moran’s I nearer its null expectation means less global residual association under the chosen weights, not necessarily better overall prediction. A model can improve one metric while worsening the other.

ggplot(model_log, aes(x = cv_rmse, y = moran_out_of_fold, label = model)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_text(nudge_y = 0.008, size = 3, check_overlap = TRUE) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar()) +
  labs(
    title = "Prediction error and residual clustering",
    x = "Cross-validated RMSE",
    y = "Moran’s I of out-of-fold residuals"
  )


These comparisons hold the sample, fold assignment, and neighbor weights constant. They remain subject to the timing limitation of the incident features and do not establish performance on a future city’s housing market.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: What to do when errors cluster
text:
What to do when errors cluster
Use the map to form a specific hypothesis:







Possible explanation
Feature to investigate




Access to transit differs
Distance to stations or nearby service availability


Parks or other amenities differ
Nearby park area or distance to amenities


Recorded incidents differ
Buffer counts or distances to incidents


Neighborhood-wide price levels differ
Carefully defined neighborhood fixed effects


A relationship changes by place
An interaction, such as floor area × neighborhood


Housing quality is missing
Building condition or other available property attributes



Refit and record both CV RMSE and Moran’s I. The residual map suggests questions; it does not supply a causal explanation by itself. Do not repeatedly tune features against a final test set.
The choice of five neighbors is also a modeling choice. It captures one local scale. A larger k examines a broader area; a smaller k is more local and may be noisier. Compare I across candidate models using the same definition, and label any sensitivity analysis that changes k.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Spatial lag diagnostics are not spatial lag predictors
text:
Spatial lag diagnostics are not spatial lag predictors
The diagnostic lag.listw(w_knn, residuals) summarizes neighboring errors after outcomes are known. A spatial lag model of the outcome has a different form:
\[
y = \rho Wy + X\beta + \varepsilon.
\]
Here Wy contains neighboring outcome values. For this assignment, the rule is to build spatial predictors from X, not from neighboring sale prices Y.
The risk is leakage: computing a price-based neighborhood feature from the complete dataset can carry validation outcomes into training features. Test prices are also unavailable, so a feature requiring them cannot be constructed at prediction time.
Spatial lag models are not universally incapable of prediction. They require appropriate estimation, prediction procedures, and information assumptions. Likewise, genuinely prior sale prices can be useful in other applications when carefully restricted to information available at the time. Those are separate methods, not a reason to ignore the assignment’s rule.
An allowed non-price feature can still leak future information if its date is after the prediction date. Always ask: Would I know this value when making the prediction?

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
section: Where does the model fail worst?
text:
Where does the model fail worst?
Overall RMSE can hide uneven performance. Inspect errors by price range, location, property size, and other relevant groups. A model that is acceptable for expensive houses may be poor for cheaper homes, or the reverse.
The following uses out-of-fold predictions from the kNN-distance model so each prediction was made without training on that property’s fold.

error_audit <- model_data %>%
  mutate(
    prediction = evaluations$KNN_distance$oof_pred,
    residual = sale_price - prediction,
    overvaluation_pct = 100 * (prediction - sale_price) / sale_price,
    price_group = cut(
      sale_price,
      breaks = c(-Inf, 100000, 250000, 500000, Inf),
      labels = c("Up to $100k", "$100k–$250k", "$250k–$500k", "Over $500k")
    )
  ) %>%
  group_by(price_group) %>%
  summarize(
    n = n(),
    rmse = sqrt(mean(residual^2)),
    mean_residual = mean(residual),
    median_overvaluation_pct = median(overvaluation_pct),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

error_audit %>% knitr::kable(digits = 2)

Here positive overvaluation_pct means predicted price is above actual price. That uses the opposite subtraction from the residual definition, so the column name makes the direction explicit.
Grouping by actual price is a post-prediction diagnostic, not a predictor. Price is available for the labeled training observations but unavailable for the competition test houses.
Percentage errors provide context that dollar RMSE lacks. A $30,000 overprediction is 30% of a $100,000 house’s price but 3% of a $1 million house’s price. Inspect sample sizes, outliers, and geographic distributions before making claims about systematic harm. Group error patterns alone do not establish the cause of inequity.

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Assignment 5: house-price prediction in Chicago
The October 16 lecture introduces a team competition using approximately 23,000 single-family sales from 2023–2025. The assignment applies the same workflow in Chicago rather than Philadelphia.







Item
Requirement described in the lecture




Team
Four members, one team submission


Due date
Friday, October 30, 2026


Outcome
Sale price, kept in dollars


Training file
chicago_train.csv, with prices


Test file
chicago_test.csv, without prices


Spatial CRS
EPSG 3435, Illinois East State Plane in US survey feet


Prediction file
team_XX_predictions.csv


Report
Every teammate renders the analysis on their own portfolio and submits that link on Canvas, following the assignment template


Model log
Each model’s CV RMSE and Moran’s I


Error analysis
Where predictions fail worst and whose homes are overvalued



The lecture connects the task to concerns about regressive property assessments discussed in the Chicago Tribune’s The Tax Divide. The policy question is not only whether average prediction error is small, but whether errors burden cheaper homes disproportionately.

What CV and the test set tell us
CV estimates performance using repeated held-out parts of the labeled training data. The instructor’s test score evaluates predictions on a separate set whose prices were withheld.
A large difference between CV and test RMSE is a reason to investigate leakage, overfitting, different data distributions, spatial dependence, preprocessing inconsistencies, and sampling variability. It is not automatic proof of leakage. The test RMSE is an observed score on that test sample, not a universal truth about every future prediction.


Training rules and test predictions
Outcome-based cleaning can be applied to training sales when justified, but test prices are unknown. Do not drop test rows simply because a predictor is missing; use a documented strategy learned from the training data. The required prediction file should retain the expected test identifiers and one prediction per required row.
The Chicago files were not part of this lecture example, so the Philadelphia column names should not be assumed to match their schema. Inspect the actual assignment data and template before writing the Chicago data-processing code.


Individual understanding
The lecture says Q7 on October 30 asks about the team’s own model: which features were used and why, how CV and test RMSE differ, and where the model fails worst. Every member needs to understand the shared model rather than only their own code contribution.

text:
Terms and syntax to remember







Term or code
Meaning

title: Week 7: Where Is the Model Wrong?
text:
Questions to check my understanding

How is a point buffer different from a census tract boundary?
What is fixed in a buffer count, and what is fixed in a kNN distance feature?
Why can two houses with zero buffer counts still have different kNN distances?
Why do we project Philadelphia data to EPSG 2272 before buffering?

Does scales::squish change the errors used in RMSE?
Which neighbors are used for the incident feature, and which for Moran’s I?
What does row standardization do when a house has five neighbors?
Is a spatial lag the value in the previous table row?
Why do two negative deviations contribute positively to Moran’s I?
Why does the five-house example change when the weights change?
Does I = 0.26 mean 26% of errors are clustered?
What stays fixed and what gets shuffled in moran.mc()?
Why is a small permutation p-value not enough to judge a model?
Can RMSE improve while residual clustering gets worse?
Why must the residual vector stay aligned with the neighbor list?
Why can nearby validation houses make random-fold CV optimistic for new areas?
Can a crime feature leak information even though it does not use prices?
Why are negative residuals relevant when looking for overvalued homes?
