title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text: These standalone notes summarize Dr. Elizabeth Delmelle’s October 23, 2026 lecture. Numerical results below come from the supplied lecture text.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
A model can predict reasonably well overall but still make similar mistakes in certain neighborhoods. This week asks:

Where are the mistakes? Use Local Moran’s I (LISA).
What might explain them? Build spatial features and test them.
Who is affected? Consider how predictions are used, even when they are accurate.

These notes summarize Dr. Elizabeth Delmelle’s week8_slides.html, dated October 23, 2026. The examples concern Philadelphia house prices and the RealPage classroom discussion. All numerical results come from the slides.
This is a standalone study note, separate from Assignment 5. It does not load CSV files, run models, or require assignment data. The weekly-notes/week08-data/ folder is reserved for weekly-note data; no files from it are needed to render this summary.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
1. Start with residuals
\[
\text{Residual} = \text{actual price} - \text{predicted price}
\]








Residual
Meaning
Example




Positive
The model underpredicts
Actual $300,000, predicted $250,000: residual +$50,000


Negative
The model overpredicts
Actual $300,000, predicted $350,000: residual −$50,000



The lecture uses out-of-fold residuals: each house’s prediction comes from a model trained without that house’s validation fold. This gives a more useful check of prediction performance than errors on the training data.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
2. Global Moran’s I versus LISA
Spatial autocorrelation means nearby observations tend to have related values. Here, the values are prediction errors.








Method
Output
Main question




Global Moran’s I
One statistic for the dataset
Do similar errors cluster overall?


Local Moran’s I, used in LISA analysis
One statistic per house
Where are the clusters and spatial outliers?



LISA stands for Local Indicators of Spatial Association. In this lecture, it refers to analysis using Local Moran’s I.

How Local Moran’s I works
First center the residuals: \(z_i = e_i - \bar e\), where \(e_i\) is a house’s residual and \(\bar e\) is the mean residual.
\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2}\sum_j w_{ij}z_j,
\qquad
m_2 = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i z_i^2.
\]
Think of it as my centered error × my neighbors’ average centered error, divided by a common scale.

Same signs produce a positive local statistic: similar errors nearby.
Opposite signs produce a negative local statistic: a house differs from its neighbors.
A value near zero indicates a weak local product; significance still needs testing.

The lecture uses each house’s five nearest sales as neighbors. Row-standardized weights (style = "W") give each of those five neighbors weight 1/5, so their spatial lag is their average centered residual.
In the five-house example, house A has \(z_A = 84\) and a neighbor average of 64, measured in thousands of dollars. With \(m_2 = 4{,}584\):
\[
I_A = \frac{84 \times 64}{4{,}584} \approx 1.17.
\]
The average local statistic is about 0.72, equal to global Moran’s I with these row-standardized weights. The earlier value of 0.60 used different weights. Compare models using the same neighborhood definition and weights.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
3. Read the four LISA groups
The first word describes the house; the second describes its neighbors.








Group
Pattern
What to investigate




High–High (HH)
High residual surrounded by high residuals
A neighborhood feature the model may be missing, such as an amenity


Low–Low (LL)
Low residual surrounded by low residuals
A neighborhood feature the model may be missing, such as vacancy


High–Low (HL)
High residual surrounded by low residuals
An unusual house or a data problem


Low–High (LH)
Low residual surrounded by high residuals
An unusual house or a data problem



High and low mean above and below the mean residual. When that mean is near zero, HH roughly identifies underpredicted pockets and LL roughly identifies overpredicted pockets. Always check the actual residual signs before making that interpretation.
HH and LL are clusters. HL and LH are spatial outliers. These patterns suggest questions; they do not prove what caused the errors.

Significance and the R functions
The slides use 499 permutations and a 0.01 significance threshold to distinguish flagged patterns from those labeled “Not significant.” Permutations compare the observed local association with randomized reference patterns.







R function
Purpose




knearneigh(..., k = 5)
Find the five nearest neighboring sales


knn2nb()
Convert those neighbors into a neighbor list


nb2listw(..., style = "W")
Create weights that sum to one for each house


lag.listw(w, z)
Calculate each house’s weighted neighbor average


localmoran_perm(resid, w, nsim = 499)
Calculate local statistics and permutation tests



Keep residuals in exactly the same row order as the spatial weights. Testing thousands of houses can produce chance flags, even with a small threshold. “Not significant” also does not mean the prediction is accurate.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
section: 4. Turn a map pattern into a feature
text:
4. Turn a map pattern into a feature
Operationalizing means turning an idea into something measurable. For example, “near crime” could mean three different things:








Feature
What it measures
Main limitation




Buffer count
Number of incidents within a fixed radius, such as 660 feet
Results depend on the radius; many houses may have zero


Nearest distance
Distance to the single closest incident
One unusual incident can dominate


kNN mean distance
Average distance to the nearest \(k\) incidents
Results depend on \(k\); distant incidents still count



A higher count means more incidents within the buffer. A larger distance means incidents are farther away. A zero count does not tell us how far away the nearest incident is.
Use a projected coordinate system with appropriate distance units. The Philadelphia example uses EPSG 2272, in US survey feet.
Two different uses of neighbors: the incident features find nearby incidents; LISA finds nearby houses and compares their residuals.

Why log a distance?
Logging emphasizes proportional changes. Moving from 100 to 500 feet is a fivefold increase, while moving from 5,000 to 5,400 feet is only an 8% increase. Both add 400 feet, but their log changes differ greatly.
log(distance) requires a positive distance. Check for zeros, including coincident locations, before using it.
Choose a small, justified list of radii or \(k\) values, then compare their cross-validation RMSE using the same folds. Lower RMSE means smaller prediction errors overall. In the slides, the four feature versions have very similar RMSE values, so there is no large performance improvement to claim.

The lecture tests whether neighborhood vacancy explains Low–Low pockets.

Use this workflow:

Fit a model and calculate out-of-fold residuals.
Check global Moran’s I and map the LISA groups.
Ask what might explain a cluster.
Measure that idea and add it as a feature.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
6. Who bears the model’s mistakes?
If predicted values were used for tax assessments, overprediction could create an excessive tax burden. The lecture finds LL classifications in 4.48% of sales in the lowest tract-income quintile, compared with 0.459% in the highest.
This suggests uneven error patterns worth investigating. Tract income describes an area, not an individual household, and these predictions are not actual tax bills.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
section: 7. RealPage: accuracy is only one question
text:
7. RealPage: accuracy is only one question
The slides describe software that recommends rents using public information, a landlord’s own records, and competitors’ nonpublic rental information. A manager may accept or override the recommendation.
The classroom debate focuses on pooled competitor data and how independently landlords make pricing decisions. Critics argue that these systems can enable price coordination; defenders emphasize efficiency and human discretion. These are competing positions presented in the lecture.
In the classroom role-play, an RFP (request for proposals) describes a hypothetical rent-pricing project. Students discuss public-data predictions, pooled private rent rolls, daily recommendations, default acceptance, block-level geography, revenue optimization, competitor benchmarking, and confidentiality. The exercise illustrates how technical ability, business incentives, legal constraints, and ethical judgment can lead to different decisions.
The lecture frames the discussion with three questions:

What goes into the data, and who supplied it? Public information and competitors’ private records raise different concerns.
Who acts on the prediction, and can they say no? Default acceptance can strongly shape decisions.
Who pays when it is wrong—or right? A model that accurately predicts willingness to pay can still harm tenants when used to maximize rents.

The slides discuss Philadelphia rules and a RealPage-specific federal settlement. Treat those legal details as lecture context requiring separate verification before practical use, not as universal rules for every spatial model.

title: Week 8: Finding Local Errors and Using Models Responsibly
text:
Quick self-check

Which statistic tells me where errors cluster? Local Moran’s I, interpreted with a LISA map.
What does a negative residual mean? The prediction was too high.
What is the difference between HH and HL? HH is a cluster of similar high residuals; HL is a high residual among low neighbors.
Does lower RMSE guarantee fewer local clusters? No; the vacancy example shows why both need checking.
Does an accurate model guarantee a good outcome? No; the data, decisions, and people affected also matter.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text:
1. What is this week about?
A model can perform well overall but repeatedly make mistakes in the same neighborhood.

Find the mistakes: use global Moran’s I and LISA.
Investigate them: measure a missing neighborhood feature and test it.
Consider the consequences: ask who is affected by the predictions.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text:
2. Start with prediction errors
\[
\text{Residual} = \text{actual price} - \text{predicted price}
\]
For a house that sells for $300,000:



Prediction
Residual
Meaning

−$50,000
Overprediction: the prediction is too high



Use out-of-fold residuals: predict each house using a model trained without that house’s validation group. This checks how well the model predicts data it did not train on.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text:
3. Global Moran’s I and LISA
Spatial autocorrelation means nearby observations have related values. Here, we are studying nearby prediction errors.








Method
What it gives
Question it answers




Global Moran’s I
One number for the dataset
Do similar errors cluster overall?


Local Moran’s I (used in LISA)
One number per house
Where are the clusters and unusual houses?



LISA means Local Indicators of Spatial Association. The lecture uses each house’s five nearest sales as its neighbors.

The basic calculation
Local Moran’s I multiplies a house’s centered residual by its neighbors’ average centered residual, then divides by a common scale. A centered residual is the residual minus the mean residual.

Same signs: a positive local value, suggesting similar errors nearby.
Opposite signs: a negative local value, suggesting a house differs from its neighbors.

The lecture’s five-house example gives an average local value of 0.72, equal to global Moran’s I under the same row-standardized weights. These weights average the neighbors. Different weights can give a different result, so keep weights consistent when comparing models.


Read the four groups
The first word describes the house; the second describes its neighbors.








Group
Meaning
What to investigate




High–High
High residual among high residuals
A missing neighborhood amenity


Low–Low
Low residual among low residuals
A missing neighborhood disadvantage


High–Low
High residual among low residuals
An unusual house or incorrect data


Low–High
Low residual among high residuals
An unusual house or incorrect data



High and low are relative to the mean residual. If that mean is near zero, High–High roughly means a pocket of underprediction, and Low–Low roughly means a pocket of overprediction.
High–High and Low–Low are clusters. High–Low and Low–High are spatial outliers. Neither proves the cause of an error.
The lecture uses 499 random permutations and a 0.01 significance threshold to flag patterns. With thousands of houses, some flags can occur by chance. “Not significant” does not mean a prediction is accurate.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text:
4. Turn “near” into a measurable feature
Operationalizing means turning an idea into a number. For example, “near violent incidents” can be measured in three ways:








Method
Example
Limitation




Buffer count
Number of incidents within 660 feet
Depends on the chosen radius


Nearest distance
Distance to the closest incident
One incident can dominate


kNN mean distance
Average distance to the five closest incidents
Depends on the chosen number of neighbors



More incidents produce a higher count. Closer incidents produce a smaller distance. Use coordinates with suitable distance units; the lecture uses feet.
Logging a distance emphasizes proportional changes: 100 to 500 feet is a much bigger proportional change than 5,000 to 5,400 feet. Check that distances are positive before taking their logarithms.
Choose a few reasonable radii or neighbor counts, then compare cross-validation RMSE using the same rows and folds. RMSE measures prediction error; lower is better.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
text:
6. Why do these errors matter?
If predictions were used for property assessments, overprediction could mean an excessive tax burden.
In the lecture, 4.48% of sales in the lowest tract-income group were Low–Low, compared with 0.459% in the highest group. This suggests uneven error patterns worth investigating. These are model results, not actual tax bills; tract income also does not tell us an individual household’s income.

title: Week 8: Local Errors, Spatial Features, and RealPage
section: 7. RealPage: should we use the model?
text:
7. RealPage: should we use the model?
The lecture describes RealPage software that recommends rents using public information, landlords’ own records, and competitors’ private rental data.
The debate concerns sharing competitors’ private information and how freely managers can reject recommendations. Critics argue that this can help landlords coordinate prices. Defenders emphasize efficiency and managers’ control over final prices.
The classroom bidding exercise asks whether a consulting firm should accept, modify, or reject requests such as pooling private rent rolls, accepting recommendations by default, and maximizing revenue. It asks students to distinguish what they can build from what they are willing to sell.
Three questions guide the discussion:

Where does the data come from? Public information and competitors’ private records raise different concerns.
Who makes the decision? Can a manager meaningfully reject the recommendation?
Who bears the consequences? Renters may be harmed even when the model accurately predicts what they will pay.

Accuracy alone does not make a model’s use fair or beneficial.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
text:
In class we built a house price model for Philadelphia. Now your team does it for a city you haven’t modeled: Chicago.
The Cook County Assessor’s Office has to value every home in the county, including the vast majority that didn’t sell this year. Assessments drive property tax bills. When they’re wrong in a systematic way, some households pay more than their share. A 2017 Chicago Tribune investigation, “The Tax Divide,” found exactly that in Cook County: lower-value homes were assessed at higher shares of their worth than expensive ones.
Build a model that predicts single-family sale prices in Chicago, 2023–2025, using only the tools from this course. The file contains only features of the house itself. Everything about location is yours to build.









File
What’s in it




chicago_train.csv
About 80% of the houses, with sale prices


chicago_test.csv
The other 20%, without sale prices. You predict them; we score you.



The test houses were held out by house, not by sale, so a house that sold twice is entirely on one side. Your CV RMSE is your estimate. Your test RMSE is the truth. If they’re far apart, something leaked.
Due: Friday, October 30. All teammates renders the file on their portfolio and every member submits that link on Canvas. One teammate uploads team_XX_predictions.csv.
Individual accountability: Q7 on October 30 asks each of you about this model: which features you used and why, your CV and test RMSE, and where the model fails worst. Make sure everyone can explain all of it.

You must predict every test house, so fill NAs in a feature rather than filtering.

Transform predictors, not sale_price.



No features built from other houses’ sale prices.

Every model you tried, in order, with CV RMSE and Moran’s I. Each row has a note saying why you tried it.

Incorporate the feature engineering tricks - including the spatial ones covered these past few weeks.

Choices justified by evidence from your own analysis.

We fill the six predictors that have missing values with medians from the fitting rows. During cross-validation, we calculate those medians separately inside each fitting fold. We use the same medians to fill that fold’s held-out rows. We do not add missingness indicators or fill in test sale prices.


Exploration plots
We use the cleaned training data to see how prices relate to size, age and location. These plots help us choose what to test in the models. We then use cross-validation to see whether those choices help.
We start by looking at the price distribution. We want to see where most sales fall and how far the highest prices are from the rest. Errors on those expensive houses can have a big effect on RMSE. The labels are in millions, so $1m means $1,000,000. We are only changing the labels, not the prices.


Code

  geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = "#287D8E", color = "white") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "m")) +
  labs(x = "Sale price", y = "Sales")





Prices are right-skewed. The dollar-axis histogram retains every cleaned training sale.




Next, we compare building size with price. Do bigger houses sell for more, and how much do prices vary for houses of the same size? We multiply building_000sf by 1,000 to show square feet. The log axes make the smaller values easier to see alongside the larger ones, and transparency helps when points overlap. Our model still predicts prices in dollars. If the relationship looks curved, we have a reason to test a size transformation.


Code

  geom_point(alpha = .15, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_comma()) + scale_y_log10(labels = money) +
  labs(x = "Reported building area (square feet)", y = "Sale price (log display)")





Building size and price; both display axes are logarithmic. The regression outcome remains dollars.




We also look at price against building age. We want to see whether a straight-line relationship seems reasonable or whether we should test age squared as well. We do not remove a house just because it is old. Again, the log price axis is only for the plot.


Code
ggplot(st_drop_geometry(train), aes(building_age, sale_price)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .12, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = money) + labs(x = "Building age (years)", y = "Sale price (log display)")





Prices vary widely within building ages; age alone is not a cleaning rule.




Finally, we map the sales to see where higher and lower prices cluster. Each point is a sale, and the color shows its price. If prices vary across the city, we have a reason to test location features alongside house characteristics. The map alone cannot explain why those differences exist. We use a log color scale so a few expensive sales do not dominate the colors.


Code
ggplot(train) + geom_sf(aes(color = sale_price), size = .35, alpha = .6) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = money, name = "Sale price") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)





Cleaned training sales. Color uses a logarithmic price scale; no expensive records are hidden.




Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Houses with similar sizes sell for very different prices, so we did not expect house characteristics alone to explain everything. We started with a structure-only model, then tested squared size and age terms and an alternative using log size. The map also gave us a reason to test location features. We used cross-validation to check whether those additions helped.
We kept the unusually low and high prices because we did not have enough evidence to call them errors. That choice has consequences: expensive sales can drive dollar RMSE, while a relatively small dollar error can be a large percentage of a cheap house’s price. We return to both issues in Part 4.

Part 2: Build the model
Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes.

Build the location features
We join houses to Census tracts, calculate their distance from the Loop, and make three distance rings. The tract is a place category, like the district factor in Week 6. We use these location features without using other houses’ prices.

Prepare the tract categories
We count distinct location groups within each training tract. Tracts with fewer than 15 groups, unmatched tracts and test tracts absent from training go into “Other”. This follows the notes’ idea of pooling small categories. “Other” can combine unrelated places, so its predictions deserve care. The threshold uses location counts, not prices. Below, we display how many folds contain each tract category. A category found in only one fold would have no fitting examples when that fold is held out.

Fill missing predictors
We need a prediction for every test house, so we fill missing predictors instead of dropping test rows. Week 8 uses replace_na() and median() for this. During CV, we calculate the medians from the fitting fold only. For the final test predictions, we use medians from all cleaned training rows.
The reference argument tells the function which rows provide those medians. Writing the columns separately lets us see exactly what gets filled.


Code
fill_missing <- function(data, reference) {
  data <- st_drop_geometry(data)
  reference <- st_drop_geometry(reference)

  data %>%
    mutate(
      lotsize_acre = replace_na(lotsize_acre,
        median(reference$lotsize_acre, na.rm = TRUE)),
      num_half_baths = replace_na(num_half_baths,
        median(reference$num_half_baths, na.rm = TRUE)),
      num_fireplaces = replace_na(num_fireplaces,
        median(reference$num_fireplaces, na.rm = TRUE)),
      garage_size = replace_na(garage_size,
        median(reference$garage_size, na.rm = TRUE)),
      full_basement = replace_na(full_basement,
        median(reference$full_basement, na.rm = TRUE)),
      warmairfurnace = replace_na(warmairfurnace,
        median(reference$warmairfurnace, na.rm = TRUE))
    )
}




Create the same folds for every model
We use all cleaned training rows in ten-fold CV. In each round, nine folds fit the model and the remaining fold checks it. Each house gets a prediction from a model that did not use its sale price. We use these out-of-fold predictions for the residual maps and error analysis, as in Week 8.
Records at the same rounded coordinates stay in the same fold. This is a proxy for repeated properties because we do not have parcel IDs. It can group distinct nearby houses or miss repeat records whose coordinates differ. Nearby houses can still appear across folds.

Cross-validation and spatial weights
This loop follows Week 7. We fill missing predictors using the fitting rows before calling lm(). We keep the raw predictions, including negative values, when we calculate error. We do not replace them with zero. Negative predictions show where this linear model gives an impossible house value.


Code
cv_predictions <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))

  for (k in 1:10) {
    validation <- fold_id == k
    fitting <- fill_missing(data[!validation, ], data[!validation, ])
    validating <- fill_missing(data[validation, ], data[!validation, ])

    fit <- lm(formula, data = fitting)
    predictions[validation] <- predict(fit, newdata = validating)
  }

  predictions
}

morans_i <- function(values, weights) {
  moran(values, weights, n = length(values), S0 = Szero(weights))$I
}

coords <- st_coordinates(train)
has_duplicate_locations <- anyDuplicated(coords) > 0
house_knn <- knearneigh(
  coords, k = 5, longlat = FALSE,
  use_kd_tree = !has_duplicate_locations
)
house_nb <- knn2nb(house_knn)
weights <- nb2listw(house_nb, style = "W")


We use five nearest neighbors and row-standardized weights, as in the notes. Duplicate locations can create ties, so their ordering can affect the neighbor choice.


Compare the models
We run each formula on the same rows and folds. For each one, we subtract held-out predictions from actual prices, calculate dollar RMSE and Moran’s I, and add a row to the log. A positive residual means we predicted too low; a negative one means we predicted too high.

Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays
4A. Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?
4B. Assessors judge their work with the ratio of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model’s ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to “The Tax Divide.”
We use each training house’s out-of-fold prediction here, rather than the prediction from the final model that was fitted to that house. The errors include every cleaned training row, including negative predictions. We group prices into the fixed bands used in Week 7.

Median out-of-fold predicted/observed price ratios. Above 1 means overprediction, not a directly calculated tax bill.




4A. Among tracts with at least 10 cleaned training sales, tract 17031831900 had the highest MAE at $900,933. Its mean residual was $900,933, so our predictions were too low on average there.
Our largest individual error was record 19188: it sold for $14,250,000, but we predicted $7,829,126 when it was held out. Condition, renovations and measurement errors could contribute to the largest misses, but we cannot verify those explanations from the supplied columns. The LISA maps identify places for further investigation. We would need to check the data in those places before choosing a new neighborhood feature. Nearby houses still appear across folds, so these results do not establish performance in completely unseen areas.
4B. We split county tracts into three income groups using cutoffs of $64,413 and $94,315. The lower-income group’s median ratio was 1.075, compared with 1.001 for the higher-income group. We report group sizes, the share overpredicted and the ratio of summed predictions to summed prices too. That last measure gives more weight to expensive sales and can differ from the median individual ratio.
For sales up to $100,000, the median ratio was 2.229. That means the median proportional error in this group was 122.9% above the sale price. This is a serious weakness even though overall RMSE improved. Lower dollar RMSE does not guarantee small proportional errors for inexpensive houses. Grouping by actual prices can also produce regression-to-the-mean patterns, so this comparison alone does not prove discrimination.
We kept cheap sales instead of excluding them just because they were hard to predict. Removing bundled transactions made the training prices easier to interpret, but these diagnostics do not establish performance for the flagged test transactions. The Tax Divide investigation gives us a reason to take proportional overvaluation seriously. These are prediction errors, not actual tax bills or a causal effect of income. The Tax Divide investigation.
Tract income is not an owner’s income, and ACS estimates have sampling uncertainty. Across all input rows, 1 had no tract match. We retained those rows without borrowing income from another tract. A negative prediction also produces a negative ratio: that is a model failure, not a meaningful property valuation.


What changed for the difficult houses?
We compare the earlier tract model with the selected model on the same held-out training houses. This helps us distinguish a real improvement in prediction from simply hiding negative outputs.

Having examples in the same tract does not guarantee a sensible prediction for every combination of characteristics. We cannot label these source records as errors from a negative model output alone. We have reviewed these nonpositive outputs and retained them in the export. They remain model failures, not credible house values or evidence that their source records should be deleted.

title: Assignment 5: House Price Prediction, Chicago
section: Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)
text:
Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

We started with house characteristics, then added location because similar houses can sell for different prices across Chicago. We compared squared terms, log size, distance, rings, interactions and tract fixed effects. Adding tract-specific size slopes and an age-by-ring interaction gave the lowest CV RMSE among the tested formulas. We chose among them using the same grouped CV folds. These fitted relationships describe associations; they do not tell us what changing a house or neighborhood would cause.
Our central-air coefficient is $17,524. As beta-hat, it is the estimated price difference between the supplied central-air categories, holding the other predictors fixed. For y-hat, switching that indicator from 0 to 1 changes the predicted price by that amount. We cannot interpret it as the return from installing air conditioning because condition and renovations may also differ between houses.
We would not give this model to the Assessor for operational use yet. It improves on the baseline, but the residual maps and LISA results show where further checks are needed. Dollar RMSE can hide large proportional errors for inexpensive houses. Income-group comparisons help us describe that concern, but tract income is not an owner’s income and cannot establish individual fairness.
We removed bundled transactions rather than guessing how to divide their prices. We kept both price tails because we could not justify excluding them. Grouping rounded coordinates helps with repeated sales, but verified parcel IDs would be better. Our CV score also influenced model selection, so it is not an independent final test. Before using this model for assessments, we would evaluate a later year and held-out geographic areas, verify condition and transaction details, and investigate impossible predictions. We would follow Week 8’s approach of checking residual clusters and measuring a plausible missing feature before adding it. We should not assume a more complicated model will fix every error.
